# TO THE BENEVOLENT
### & Learned Reader.

You have before you, friend Reader, a work of ancient faith among the Hebrews and of great authority. The author of this rhythmic work <note>original: "Operis Rythmici." This refers to a text written in verse or with a specific meter, a common pedagogical tool in medieval Hebrew scholarship.</note> concerning the method of commentaries upon the Holy Scripture is **Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra**, who, on account of his distinguished learning and wisdom, is called preeminently <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν (kat’ exochen). This phrase means "the one who stands out" or "par excellence."</note> "the wise." The discourse on the soul, which was composed as a patchwork <note>original: "centonem." In literature, a *cento* is a work created by assembling fragments from various sources to create a new narrative; here, it refers to a thematic compilation of mystical excerpts.</note> drawn from the **Zohar** <note>The *Zohar* (Radiance) is the foundational work of Jewish mystical thought, known as Kabbalah, traditionally attributed to the circle of Shimon bar Yochai.</note>, was compiled by
->Rabbi Israel<-

<summary>In this preface, the editor introduces the reader to the two primary texts of the volume: a guide to biblical commentary by the 12th-century polymath Abraham Ibn Ezra and a compilation of mystical teachings on the soul derived from the Zohar.</summary>
<keywords>Abraham Ibn Ezra, Zohar, Rabbi Israel, Kabbalah, biblical commentary, Jewish philosophy, soul, Cento</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the sentence from the previous page, identifying "Rabbi Israel" as the compiler of the mystical text and providing publication history for the Zohar.</meta>

Rabbi Israel, son of Rabbi Moses. His work exists in a printed edition from Lublin from the year 352 of the minor count <note>The "minor count" (Hebrew: *Lishnat Perat Katan*) is a system for recording years in the Hebrew calendar that omits the thousands. The year 352 corresponds to the Hebrew year 5352, or 1592 AD.</note> among his collections under the title **Perfect Together** <note>original Hebrew: תמים יחדיו (*Tamim Yachdav*)</note>; these are joined to the new **Zohar** printed in Cracow in the year 1603. The *Zohar*, moreover, is a most famous book among the Jews, which they believe was written before the compilation of the **Talmud** <note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and Gemara; it was compiled between the 3rd and 8th centuries, whereas the Zohar appeared in the late 13th century, though attributed to earlier sages.</note>. We have added notes from the *Zohar* edition published at Cremona in the year 1558. We have also employed other classic Hebrew doctors <note>Referring to authoritative rabbinic scholars and teachers of the Jewish tradition.</note> so that their teachings might be more clearly understood; for this reason, it also seemed fitting to translate those points from the philosophy of **Plato** which accord with their own dogmas.

Thus, once the snares of that nation have been uncovered, there will be less danger and caution will be easier; for in vain is the net cast before the eyes of those with wings <note>original: "frustra enim iactatur rete ante oculos pennatorum." This is a reference to Proverbs 1:17, suggesting that once a trap is visible, it is easily avoided.</note>. Furthermore, from the very opinions accepted among the Jews, you will be able to argue against them—taking the straps, as the saying goes, from the ox itself <note>original: "ex ipso... boue lora sumere." A Latin idiom meaning to use someone's own arguments or tools against them.</note>.

One thing, it seems, must be said beforehand for your scholarly consideration: that which Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger (61–113 AD), a lawyer and author in ancient Rome.</note> wrote to Maximus when he was departing for Athens: *Let there be a respect for antiquity in your eyes; let it be given to their legends as well.* <note>The author is urging the reader to respect the age and traditional stories of the texts being studied, even if they seem mythical.</note>

If this first taste of my youth should please you, friend reader, then recognize here the fruit of a son, which a father's Senatorial hand has cultivated.

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page transitions from Joseph de Voysin’s personal preface and dedication to his father to the official ecclesiastical approval (approbatio) from the University of Paris, which was a legal and religious requirement for publishing such works in 17th-century France.</meta>

# APPROVAL.

We, the undersigned Doctors of the sacred Faculty of Theology of Paris, have read the *Cabalistic Disputation* of Rabbi Israel regarding the Soul, written in Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldaïce." In this period, "Chaldean" was the standard term for the Aramaic language.</note>, as well as the rhythmic work of Rabbi Abraham Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167) was a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar, poet, and grammarian.</note> regarding the methods by which the Hebrews are accustomed to interpret the Law <note>The "Law" refers to the Torah.</note>, published in Rabbinic [Hebrew]; which the noble man **Joseph de Voysin** of Bordeaux has expressed word-for-word in English <note>original: "latine" (Latin). In keeping with the instructions to translate all text into English, the translation itself is the subject here.</note>, with Scholarly Annotations <term>Scholia: marginal or explanatory notes used in ancient and medieval manuscripts to clarify the text.</term> added from the *Zohar* and other books of the Rabbis and the Platonists. We have found his translation to be sincere and entirely consistent with the Chaldean and Rabbinic text. Nevertheless, so that these authors—who are otherwise useful to scholars—should not go forth in a mutilated form, and lest the unwary reader should stumble, we have, by way of censure, noted those places which wander from the path of truth and the Christian faith. From our house of study <note>original: "è Musis nostris," literally "from our Muses," a scholarly idiom for a place of learning or a library.</note> in the year of our Lord 1635, on the twenty-third day of the month of January.

->H. PARENT. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; D'AMONT.<-

<summary>This page contains the official certification from the University of Paris theologians, authorizing the publication of Voysin's translations of Rabbi Israel and Ibn Ezra while noting that potentially "heretical" passages have been flagged for the reader.</summary>
<keywords>Approval, Faculty of Theology of Paris, Cabala, Rabbi Israel, Abraham ibn Ezra, Joseph de Voysin, Zohar, Rabbinic literature, Platonism, censorship, 1635</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal ecclesiastical review from the Faculty of Theology at Paris. While the previous page provided the general "approval" (approbatio) for Joseph de Voysin’s work, this page provides the "censure" (censura)—not in the sense of a total ban, but a critical review pointing out specific theological errors in the Jewish texts to ensure Christian readers are not misled by non-Christian doctrines.</meta>

### The Review of the Doctors.

Just as the books of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note>, when they appeared with their blemishes and errors, expressed the greater mental blindness of the Idolaters; so too the scholarly works <note>original: "lucubrationes," literally "work by lamplight," signifying deep study.</note> of the Jews—upon whom Christ, the Sun of truth and justice, has not shone—reveal more clearly the darkness of ignorance that overwhelms them through a lack of true light, even as they are published for the public exactly as they were written by their authors. For this reason, regarding the complete edition and the version of these two short works by **Rabbi Israel** and **R. Aben Ezra** produced by the noble man **Lord de Voysin** <note>Joseph de Voysin (c. 1610–1685) was a French Hebraist and theologian.</note>, we have approved his plan and intention in adding scholarly notes <term>Scholia: explanatory comments or annotations intended to clarify a difficult passage in a text.</term> to each individual chapter. We did this so that if there were anything ingenious, useful, or worthy of knowledge in them—especially in that synopsis of everything the Jews have believed regarding the soul, which he has compiled so eruditely—we would not deprive our readers of it. At the same time, if anything in the opinions of the Jews or others were discordant with reason, or based on myths, or strayed from the faith, or bypassed the standard of Christian justice, we have marked them out piece by piece, so that no one might stumble upon them.

Chapter 1, page 5. Regarding those things mentioned from the *Zohar* <note>The *Zohar* is the foundational work in the literature of Jewish mystical thought known as Kabbalah.</note> concerning the book brought by the angel Raziel to Adam <note>The *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh* (Book of Raziel the Angel) is a collection of mystical and magical secrets supposedly given to the first man.</note>, the entire doctrine of which was hidden even from the higher Angels: [this must be rejected] unless it refers to special revelations made to the First Parent <note>original: "Protoparenti," a traditional term for Adam as the father of the human race.</note> regarding the mysteries of grace.

<summary>This page contains the "Censura Doctorum," an official theological review that justifies publishing Jewish mystical texts by arguing that their "errors" serve to highlight the superior truth of Christianity. It specifically begins to address and "correct" mystical claims from the Zohar regarding the Book of Raziel.</summary>

<keywords>Censorship, Joseph de Voysin, Rabbi Israel, Ibn Ezra, Zohar, Angel Raziel, Adam, Jewish Soul, Christian Theology, Paris Faculty of Theology</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Censure" or critical review by the Doctors of the Faculty of Theology at Paris regarding Joseph de Voysin’s edition of Jewish texts. While the previous page ended by warning that readers should not "stumble" upon errors, this page lists specific theological deviations found in the works of Rabbi Israel, the Zohar, and Rabbi Meir Aldabi.</meta>

...[if they] are accepted, they are mythical <note>original: "fabulosa sunt." The censors are warning that these Jewish traditions should be treated as fables rather than theological truths.</note>.

### Chapter 1, page 2.
Erroneously, and against the true principle of creation—which is a production out of nothing <term>creatio ex nihilo: the Christian doctrine that God created the universe from nothing, rather than from pre-existing matter or His own substance.</term>—**Rabbi Israel** indicates that the elements were produced from light created by God.

### In the notes on pages 176 and 177.
The author of the **Zohar** <note>The primary text of Jewish Kabbalah, which the censors here treat with skepticism.</note> rashly invents the idea that **Adam**, by the benefit of a created light, was able to see from one end of the world to the other. He rather foolishly adds that this light—which according to Genesis 1 is the day itself—was hidden away because of the sins of men. No less ignorantly does he confuse this present light with the light of the world to come.

In the same place, **Rabbi Meir Aldabi** <note>A 14th-century Jewish philosopher and author of "The Paths of Faith" (Shevilei Emunah).</note> challenges the supreme wisdom of God—which fashioned all things in "weight and measure" <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "But thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note>—when he claims that the created light was so great that creatures could not endure it, and that only a seventh part of it was left remaining.

### Page 179.
The opinion of **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher. The censors reject his ideas as being in conflict with "true" (Christian) philosophy.</note> opposes true philosophy.

### Page 185.
The **Zohar** says that God made a single point in the head, or in Himself, in which He formed the ideas of the world; these claims indeed shatter the eternal perfection and immutability of God <note>The censors argue that if God "formed ideas" within Himself at a specific point, it implies He changed or had a beginning, which contradicts the doctrine that God is unchanging and eternal.</note>.

### Page 189.
Regarding that verse of **Psalm 110** ("You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek"), the same **Zohar** unskillfully attributes it to **Abraham**, whose priesthood was by no means eternal <note>Christian theology identifies the "eternal priest" in this Psalm as Jesus Christ, not Abraham.</note>.

<summary>This page contains a list of theological corrections issued by Parisian censors regarding Jewish mystical interpretations of creation, the nature of Adam's sight, and the priesthood of Melchizedek.</summary>
<keywords>creatio ex nihilo, Zohar, Adam, Genesis, Rabbi Israel, Rabbi Meir Aldabi, Iamblichus, Psalm 110, Melchizedek, Abraham, Kabbalah, censorship</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Censure" or critical review by the Faculty of Theology at Paris. Having previously addressed general errors in Jewish texts edited by Joseph de Voysin, the censors now list specific theological deviations found on pages 193 through 211 of his work, focusing on the Zohar, the Talmud, and the philosophy of Maimonides.</meta>

### Page 193. 
Concerning the sun being made from dust which is beneath the throne of glory <note>original: "solio gloriæ." In Jewish tradition, the *Kisseh ha-Kavod* or Throne of Glory is the place from which souls and certain celestial elements originate.</note>; this is an absurd and fabricated opinion.

### Page 201. 
That all things are dust and shall eventually return to it; if the **Zohar** <note>The primary text of Jewish Kabbalah, often viewed with suspicion by 17th-century Christian theologians for its mystical interpretations.</note> maintains this regarding anything other than mixed bodies <term>mixed bodies: in medieval natural philosophy, these are complex physical objects composed of the four elements, which were believed to decompose back into their components, unlike simple elements or celestial matter.</term>, it is false and erroneous, as is the mythical story it tells concerning the dust of the holy house <note>Refers to the Temple in Jerusalem.</note>.

### Pages 204, 205, and 206. 
What the author of the book entitled *The Cedars of Lebanon* <note>original: "Cedri Libani." This refers to a collection of Jewish traditions or Midrashim.</note> relates regarding the council held by God with the Angels, and their opinions concerning the making of man and his sin, are mythical stories, contrary to Scripture, and serve to evade the testimonies regarding the mystery of the Trinity <note>Christian censors often argued that when God says "Let us make man" in Genesis, He is speaking within the Trinity; they viewed the Jewish interpretation of God consulting angels as a way to avoid this Christian doctrine.</note>.

### Pages 208 and 209. 
The opinion of the **Babylonian Talmud** regarding the immense size of **Adam’s** body, and its shrinking after his sin, is a fiction.

### Page 210. 
**Rabbi Maimon** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the most influential Jewish philosopher of the Middle Ages.</note> asserts that **Adam**, before his sin, required no sense or bodily assistance for his intellectual knowledge; but in this he is foolish, and he does away with the wondrous harmony between the body and the soul.

### Page 211. 
Absurdly, and against the nature of successive things, the **Zohar** affirms that when the world was founded, God created at the same time the seven days, seven weeks, seven years, and the seven thousand years of the world's duration. It rashly fixes this limit of seven thousand years upon the world, and in the same place repeats the old error concerning the angels' bod[ies]— <note>The original Latin "cor-" is a catchword for "corporibus" (bodies), likely referring to the controversial idea that angels possess a form of subtle physical body.</note>

->Cabalistic Disputation<-

...parts <note>original: *capitibus*; the conclusion of the word from the previous page, literally "heads" or "principal parts."</note> which, by standing together and being composed with one another, form one single Body. Observing this work, David exclaims in Psalm 104, verse 24: **"How magnificent are your works, O Lord!"** <note>original: *Quam magnificata sunt opera tua Deus*</note>

From this, the communion <note>The shared essence or connection.</note> of the Law and the world with man is also evident. For it is certain that in the first formation of humanity, a universal cause indeed concurred; that is, heaven and earth are moved for their sake, and they operate through them, and they abundantly satisfy one another, continually preserving their order. By their movements, one is served by the other <note>original: *desertur*; likely a scribal error for *deservitur* (served) or *defertur* (carried), as the context implies mutual support between the celestial and terrestrial realms.</note>, so that through these two, the happiness of man is perfected. This is all the more true because the divine Law confirms this perfection, as seen in Leviticus 26:3: *If you walk in my commandments, etc. I will give you rains, etc.*

### Concerning the Union of the Blessed God, the Law, and Israel.

*Three levels cling to each other: the Holy Blessed God, the Law, and Israel.*

# Cabalistic Disputation

...the Blessed God, the Law <term>Law<gloss>Torah</gloss></term>, and Israel are each joined together one to another, both secretly and openly. The Blessed God, according to His degree, is both secret and open; the Law, according to its degree, is also secret and open; and likewise Israel, according to its degree, is secret and open. This is just as it is written in Psalm 146, verse 19: <note>original: *Annuntians verba sua Iacob, iustitias & iudicia sua Israёl*. In the Latin Vulgate numbering used here, this is Psalm 146; in modern Bibles, it is Psalm 147:19.</note> **"He declares His words to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments to Israel."** These two degrees—Jacob and Israel—one of which is secret and the other open, in what do they differ?

Whoever is circumcised and marked with the holy name <note>A reference to the *Brit Milah* (covenant of circumcision), which in Cabalistic thought serves as a physical "seal" of the Divine Name on the person.</note> is granted the "open" words of the Law. That is, they teach him the principles of the alphabet, the beginnings of the chapters, and the basic matter of the commandments of the Law, and nothing more, until he has ascended to another degree. This is why the verse first says: "He declares His words to Jacob"—and rightly so—but "His statutes and His judgments to Israel." These latter things are the secrets of the Law <term>secrets of the Law<gloss>Sod</gloss></term>, the ordinances of the Law, and the mysteries of the Law, which must not be revealed except to those established in the superior degree, as is proper. For if anyone should hand over even the smallest letter of the Law to one who is not circumcised, it is the same as if he were to lay waste to the world and deny the name of the Blessed God—

Cabalistic Disputation

When the world was created, nothing was firm or stable until it came into His mind to create man, who would devote himself to the <term>Law<gloss>Torah</gloss></term>, and for whose sake the world stood firm. Now, whoever applies himself to the study of the Law with all his strength, he stabilizes the world. The <note>original: *Deus benedictus*; a Latin rendering of the Hebrew *Ha-Kadosh Barukh Hu* (The Holy One, Blessed be He).</note> Blessed God looked upon the Law and created the world; man devotes himself to the Law and stabilizes the world. It is established, therefore, that the work and basis of the whole world is the Law; furthermore, in the same place it says: Blessed is the man who meditates on the Law continually, for he himself sustains the world.

### Kabbalistic Disputation

### Concerning the Soul

->The Spirit<-

The spirit is the model of the **greater world** <term>macrocosm <note>original: *mundus maior*. In Cabalistic and Hermetic thought, the "greater world" is the universe or the divine realm, while the "lesser world" is the human being.</note></term>; behold, when the spirit is clothed with a body, man becomes a model of both the higher and lower realms. Therefore, it is beneficial for the soul to be enclosed in this body; for in order that its power and operation may be manifest in this world, the soul requires its own instrument <note>original: *organo suo*</note>, as we have stated before. 

By descending into this world, the soul actually becomes more powerful, so that it may rule this lower world. It is equipped with both higher and lower adornments—though significantly more of the higher—so that it may be perfect in every part. For unless it were complete in respect to both higher and lower things, it would not be truly perfect. 

Before the soul glides into this world, it is a participant in the counsel of the higher dignity <note>Referring to the soul's existence in the divine presence or the celestial assembly before birth.</note>. However, within the body, it is perfected and completed by means of this lower world. When the soul departs from the body, it is perfected with the perfection of two worlds—the higher and the lower—provided that the man fears his God and possesses a spirit made perfect by every good thing. The soul receives this benefit and true perfection by having descended into this world, as it is written in the **Zohar** in the section "And Jacob lived" <note>original: *Vayechi*; refers to the portion of the Zohar commenting on Genesis 47:28.</note>: "When the soul is perfected in this world,"

# Cabalistic Disputation

Rav Chasda lived seventy-two years. Rabba lived only forty. In Rav Chasda’s house, there were two wedding celebrations <note>original: *Epithalamia*; songs or poems written for a bride and groom, here representing festive occasions.</note>; in Rabba’s house, there were two bereavements <note>original: *orbitates*; the loss of children or close family members, indicating a house of mourning.</note>. Rav Chasda used to complain that fine flour <term>simila: The highest quality of wheat flour, usually reserved for the wealthy or for sacred offerings.</term> was not even sought after for free to feed the dogs <note>This implies such extreme abundance that even the finest food was treated as common waste.</note>. Rabba, however, complained that even common barley could not be found to feed a human being.

Do these words not align with the principles of those who claim that the alignment of the stars <term>aspectum astrorum: The geometric positions and relationships between planets at a person's birth, believed in astrology to dictate one's "Mazal" or fortune.</term> exerts a great, dominating power over human beings? This stands in opposition to what we established at the beginning as a true principle: that the Blessed God said to the world: “O World, you and your laws shall not endure, except through the Law <note>original: *lex*; refers to the Torah, the divine instruction of the Jewish faith.</note> in which one must be constantly occupied.” 

And this is the love with which He loved us and set us apart from other nations, and called us sons, servants, and brothers, as has been said. Add to this the continuous union that exists between the people of God, the Blessed God, and His Law; for as was stated above, the entire universe was created only for the sake of Israel, so that they might be occupied with the Law. Otherwise, the world would return to nothingness. Through the Law of God, a human is able to rule over the entire array of the heavens. Yet, the facts mentioned above <note>The author is pointing out the paradox: if the Law allows one to rule the stars, why did the righteous Rabba suffer poverty and a short life while Rav Chasda prospered?</note> seem to contradict these principles.

### M iij

# Cabalistic Disputation

...you have joined a good intention with a good explanation; you have found favor and good understanding before God and men, and you have done what is good in the eyes of the Lord and of men.

I have called this work *Tamim Yachdav* <note>original Hebrew: תמים יחדיו (*Tamim Yachdav*); meaning "Perfect Together" or "Complete in Unison."</note>—"Perfect Together"—for many reasons. First, because this name teaches the nature and quality of the work: when individual verses scattered here and there are set each in their proper order, then they are "perfect together." Second, because we often explain a certain verse at length, from which other verses are also explained; once collected and mutually adhering to one another, they will be "perfect together" in turn. Furthermore, the name is truly applied because of the "open" and the "arcane" <note>original: *apertum & arcanum*; referring to the dual nature of scripture containing both plain, literal meanings and hidden, mystical secrets.</note>, especially since we have determined in this work to collect the readings of the Holy Bible <note>original: *Bibliorum sacrorum*</note> that are diffused here and there, explained in a simple way. When placed together, they will appear true and will be complete at the same time, by joining the open and mystical <note>original: *mysticas*</note> meanings for the reason stated above. Finally, when someone searches and seeks for something but does not find it, that sought-after thing is not yet "complete," because that which is sought is missing; but when it is found, then it is called

# On Psalm 51

In Nisan, or the lunar month of March, David’s mandate <note>Referring to the royal decree for military mobilization.</note> was proclaimed throughout the entire land of Israel. Uriah, along with others, joined Joab on the seventh day of Sivan, or the lunar month of May. During the months of Sivan, Tammuz, and Ab—the lunar months of May, June, and July—they devastated the lands of the Ammonites. In Elul, or the lunar month of August, they remained stationed there; and on the twenty-fourth day of Elul, the incident with Bathsheba took place. On the Day of Propitiations <term>Day of Propitiations <note>original Latin: "Die propitiationum." It means you shall not die by the hand of Dumah <note>In Jewish tradition, Dumah is the angel in charge of the souls of the dead and the officer of Gehenna (purgatory/hell). ### For if you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it.
<note>original Latin: "Quoniam si voluisses sacrificium dedissem utique." This is verse 16 of Psalm 51 (or 50 in the Vulgate numbering).</note>

Why does God not want a sacrifice to be offered to him; yet look, did he not ordain sacrifices for sinners, so that they might offer them and have their sins forgiven? Indeed, David is speaking here to *Elohim*: <note>In Hebrew theology, the name *Elohim* is often associated with God’s attribute of Justice and Judgment, whereas the name *Jehovah* (the Tetragrammaton) is associated with Mercy and Compassion.</note> however, a sacrifice is not offered to the name *Elohim*, but to *Jehovah*. For offerings are not made to the Master of Judgment on account of the severity of that judgment. So it is written in Leviticus, chapter 1, verse 2: *If any of you brings an offering to Jehovah*—note that he said *Jehovah*, not to the name *Elohim*. Again in Leviticus chapter 2, verse 1: *When anyone offers an offering of a grain offering to Jehovah.* And in Leviticus chapter 22, verse 29: *A sacrifice of praise to Jehovah.* Also in Leviticus chapter 3, verse 3: *And they shall offer from the sacrifice of the peace offering as an offering to Jehovah.* 

Therefore, since David had addressed God as *Elohim*, he had to say: *If you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.* <note>David suggests that ritual animal sacrifices (holocausts) are inappropriate for the "Judge" (Elohim), who requires a different kind of restitution.</note> For offerings are not usually made to this name. Rather, the sacrifices of *Elohim* are a broken spirit, sorrow, and contri- <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the author is likely completing the thought "contrition of heart," referencing verse 17: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart."</note>

## A broken and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.
<note>original Latin: *Cor contritum & humiliatum Deus non despicies.* This is the latter half of Psalm 51:17 (Psalm 50 in the Vulgate).</note>

What is the meaning of "you will not despise"? It means that this heart is not of the category of hearts that God rejects. A prideful heart, or a heart with a haughty spirit—these are the hearts God despises. But a broken and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.

### **Do good in your good pleasure to Zion, that you may build the walls of Jerusalem.**

### **Zohar, section "These are the Judgments" [Mishpatim], column 193.**

We must consider why it says, "Do good." It seems that God has long since bestowed good things upon Zion. Is there now a new "good" to be added to those previous ones? Indeed, it is so. For behold, from the day that God (the Blessed) first set Himself to the building of the upper holy house <note>original Latin: *domus sanctæ superioris*. In the Kabbalistic tradition of the Zohar, this refers to the celestial Temple or a higher spiritual dimension of Jerusalem that serves as the blueprint for the earthly one.</note>, that specific "good" of His "good pleasure" <note>original Latin: *bona voluntas*. This translates the Hebrew *Ratzon*, referring to the highest expression of Divine Will or favor.</note> has not yet settled within that building, and therefore it is not yet completed. For when that upper "good pleasure" is finally poured out, He will "do good" and will light the lamps of that building and of that handiwork, so that not even the highest angels will be able to gaze upon the holy house and that structure. And then the whole work will be brought to perfection.

### That you may build the walls of Jerusalem.

Because from the day when He first set Himself to the building of the holy house <note>original Latin: *domus sanctæ*. This refers to the Temple.</note>, He had not built those walls until now. But if He had not yet built the walls of Jerusalem, how much less the holy house? Truly, however, the works of God are not like the works of men. 

When men are going to build a holy house, they first construct the walls of the city, and finally they build the holy house. They construct the city walls first so that they might be protected by them, and afterward they build the house. 

Not so the Blessed God: rather, He builds the temple first, and afterward—when He descends and takes up His residence in His place—then He will build the walls of Jerusalem, the walls of the city. 

And for this reason, he first said: *Do good, O Lord, in Your good pleasure to Zion.* <note>original Latin: *Benefac domine in bona voluntate tua Sion*. This refers to the inner, spiritual foundation of the sanctuary.</note> Afterward, he added: *And You shall build the walls of Jerusalem.* <note>original Latin: *Ædificabis muros Ierusalem*. This refers to the outer defenses of the city.</note> 

This is a mystery. In all the works of God, that which is outer is usually made first, and then the inner marrow <note>original Latin: *medulla*. Often used in a philosophical or mystical sense to mean the "essence" or "inner secret."</note>. But here it is not so. See in all the works of the Blessed God, in which that which is outer is made first, in the mind...

It frames this sequence as a divine "mystery" where the spiritual essence (Zion) must be established before the physical city (Jerusalem) is secured.</summary>

## Of Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra

Abraham the Spaniard <note>original: *Abraham Hispanus*. ...of the new moon, sometimes six hours pass and the Moon appears by a certain calculation, but at other times thirty hours pass during which it does not appear, even from the heights of mountains. This occurs because the motions of the Moon vary according to the position of its own sphere and the sphere of the sun, as well as the longitude and latitude of different regions.

Even if all these matters were fully explained, there still remains a great difficulty not set forth in the Law of Moses: namely, to know how many months there are in a year, and whether [the intercalation of the leap month depends] upon the ripening of the crops...

Finally, another: the world was created for the sake of the **firstfruits**, because it is said in Exodus 23: "The beginning of the firstfruits of your land."

But why is the letter *Beth* at the beginning? To teach that God is one, while created things are two: body and for- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; Ibn Ezra is likely beginning to explain that the letter *Beth* has the numerical value of two, representing the duality of the created world (matter and form) in contrast to the unity of the Creator.</note>

<summary>Ibn Ezra argues that mystical interpretations based on individual letters are subjective and secondary to the literal meaning of the text. He lists various traditional justifications for the world's creation—such as for the Torah, for the fear of God, or for the firstfruits—before beginning a philosophical explanation of why the Bible starts with the letter Beth (representing the number two).</summary>

### From the light of His good pleasure. <note>Latin: *Ex luce beneplaciti sui*. The term *beneplacitum* is used here to translate the Hebrew *Ratzon*, meaning God's favorable will or delight.</note>

In the same way, **Plato** also judges that the benevolent will of God existed as the origin and cause of the world. In the *Timaeus Locrus* <note>original: *In Timæo locro*. This refers to a work traditionally attributed to Timaeus of Locri, which heavily influenced Platonic cosmology</note>: "Wishing to make the most excellent offspring," etc. <note>original Greek: *Δηλόμενος ὢν ἄριστον γέννημα ποιεῖן*. The Greek *Δηλόμενος* (delighted/wishing) emphasizes the intentionality of creation.</note> Therefore, since God wished to produce the most beautiful offspring, he made this God—or rather, the created world—never to be destroyed by any other cause except by God, who composed it, if he should ever wish to dissolve it.

Because the world was truly created by the "good pleasure" of God, it was therefore made most perfect, says **Rabbi Joseph, son of Gikatilla** <note>original: *R. Ioseph filius Carnitolis*. Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla was a prominent 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist, author of *Sha'are Orah* (Gates of Light)</note>, just as it is written in Psalm 145, verse 16: "You open your hand and satisfy every living thing with the blessing of your good pleasure" <note>original Latin: *benedictione beneplaciti*. The Hebrew term *Ratzon* implies both "will" and "favor."</note>.

->And this is a great secret: that the Thought through which the world was created<-
->is called Will<- <note>Hebrew: *Ratzon* (רצון)</note>

### From the light.

In the *Zohar*, in the section "In the Beginning" <note>original: *in Principio*. This refers to the *Bereshit* section of the Zohar.</note>, column 82: This is the light which God created in the beginning, and it is the **light of the eye** <note>original Aramaic: *Nehora d'Eina*. In Kabbalistic thought, this represents a spiritual clarity or "primordial light" that transcends physical sight.</note>, which God showed to Adam; by it, he could look from one end of the world to the other. But when God saw the three generations of sinners that were to come—the generation of [the first] man <note>Likely referring to the generation of Enosh, traditionally associated with the start of idolatry.</note>, the generation of the Flood, and the generation of the division of languages <note>The generation of the Tower of Babel.</note>—He hid that light so that they might not make use of it. 

God gave this light to Moses from the days of his infancy, as it is written in Exodus 2, verse 2: "And she hid him for three months." When these months had passed and he was brought to Pharaoh, God then took that light away from him until he stood on Mount Sinai to receive the Law; at that time, that light was restored to him, and the children of Israel could not endure its brilliance. Exodus 34, verse 30: When Aaron and the children of Israel saw that the face of Moses was shining and **horned** <note>original: *cornutam*. # THE CABALISTS PHILOSOPHIZE
# differently concerning this
# light, as we shall now explain

->He brought forth His word from the hidden place.<-

*In the Zohar <note>The Zohar, or "Book of Splendor," is the foundational work of Jewish mystical thought, the Cabala.</note>, in the section on the beginning, column 15, regarding verse 3 of the first chapter of Genesis: And God said ("Let there be light: and there was light").*

From this point begins the discovery of hidden mysteries: how the world was created in its particulars, for up to this point it was only described in generalities. Afterward, the general returned to being both general and particular. Until this moment, the general whole was suspended in the ether <note>original: *avir*, often referring to a spiritual or primordial space</note> through the mystery of the **Infinite One** <note>original: *En Sof*, referring to God as the boundless, unknowable essence before creation.</note>. 

Once the divine power expanded into the supernal palace <note>In Cabalistic thought, the "palace" (*heikhal*) represents a stage of divine manifestation where the formless begins to take form, often associated with the name *Elohim*.</note>—the mystery of **Elohim**—the act of "saying" is recorded regarding it, as it is written: *And God said.* Indeed, in the higher realms, "saying" is not recorded explicitly, even though the word "Beginning" <note>original: *Bereshit*, the first word of Genesis.</note> is itself considered a creative utterance. 

However, it does not explicitly use the phrase "And He said" there. This "And He said" is the point where we may begin to ask and to know. This "saying" is the power that was raised up in silence from the mystery of the Infinite through the mystery of Thought. Now, this "saying" caused that palace to give birth to what it had conceived from the holy seed. It gave birth in silence, but that which was born was heard outside. The one who gave birth did so in a silence that was not heard at all; but as soon as that which was born emerged from it, it became a **Voice** that was heard outside: *Let there be light.*

That is to say: from this point begins the principle of discovering hidden things—namely, how the world was created in its particulars. For until now, it existed only in a universal sense; afterward, that which was universal began to be both universal and particular. 

The whole of the universal realm had previously hung in the void <note>original: *vacuo*, referring to the primordial space before creation</note> arising from the mystery of the **Infinite One** <note>original: *En Sof*</note>. And He said this, and He said that, so that creation might be sought after and understood in a determined and definite way. And this "saying" is the power which was raised up in secret from the mystery of the **Infinite** through the mystery of [God's] good pleasure or thought. 

And He said: now that palace <note>The supernal palace, or *Heikhal*.</note> has brought forth from the holy seed with which it was pregnant; it gave birth in secret. That which was born, however, became known on the outside. The mother gave birth in secret, so that nothing was revealed; but when that which was born finally emerged, it became the **Voice** that was heard on the outside: *Let there be light.*

From the letters **Vav** and **Yod** <note>original Hebrew: ו & י</note> comes the female and the mother, insofar as she is receptive, <note>original Latin: *patiens*, referring to the passive or "undergoing" principle that receives the active seed.</note> and this is the level of **Understanding**. <note>original Latin: *intelligentia*; in Kabbalistic thought, this corresponds to the Sephirah *Binah*, the Divine Mother.</note> This is derived from the word **Mah** <note>original Hebrew: מה (*Mah*), meaning "What" or "How."</note> in Psalm 8: *O Lord, our Lord, **how** [Mah] wonderful is your name in all the earth.* For a not dissimilar reason, the Greek philosophers spoke of male Gods and female Gods. **Plotinus**, in the *Enneads* <note>Book 3, Book 6, Chapter 8. The divine power unfolded those things which were within itself by its own light. Thus the world began to be produced in particular detail. (***And there was light***) responding to the gra- <note>The catchword "gra-" likely leads into "gradus" (step/degree) or "gratia" (grace) on the following page.</note>

Orpheus says, speaking of the highest Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus; here used to represent the supreme Divine Principle.</note>, that is:

> *All things previously hidden he soon brought forth into the breezes of grateful light,*
> *Performing wonders from his sacred heart.*
> <note>original Latin: "Omnia tecta prius mox grati in luminis auras / Extulit è sacro faciens miracula corde."</note>

By that "hidden thing," the Greeks understand the primary essence, which is the <term>archetype and ideal world</term> <note>The realm of perfect forms or ideas that serve as the blueprint for the physical world.</note>, full of the ideas of all things, which is called the "paternal deep" and the "hidden light." They say that the "first light" is the image of this essence; so Proclus says in the writings of Simplicius: <note>Proclus and Simplicius were influential Neoplatonist philosophers who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with mystical traditions.</note> *Is not this first light indeed the image of the paternal deep, and for that reason super-mundane <note>Beyond the physical world; belonging to a higher spiritual realm.</note>, because that [deep] is also thus?* <note>original Greek: μήποτε δὲ τὸ φῶς τοῦτο πρῶτον ἐστὶν εἰκὼν τοῦ πατρικοῦ βυθοῦ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ὑπερκόσμιον ὅτι καὶ ἐκεῖνο; original Latin: Num vero lumen hoc primum imago est paterni profundi, & ob id supramundanum, quoniam & illud.</note>

This light is indeed the <term>Divine Word</term> <note>original: Verbum diuinum. Referring to the "Logos," the creative speech or reason of God.</note>, which is therefore called the "first light"—even though it is light proceeding from light—because that light from which it arises is hidden, as in Psalm 18, verse 12: *He made darkness his secret place.* It is for this reason that it is called the "paternal deep." When it unfolds itself, it begets the Word and the light; thus it is said that he brought forth his Word from the hidden place: namely, from the hidden light.

The divine soul dwells in the brain; the living soul bestows dominion and honor in the heart; and the animal soul, which desires to eat and drink, dwells in the liver. <note>original Hebrew: נשמה שוכנת במוח : ונפש החייה משפעת שררה וכבוד בלב : ונפש הבהמית המתאוה לאכול ולשתות שוכנת בכבד.</note>

That is, the Soul of wisdom, which desires to worship God, resides in the brain and is called <term>Neschamah</term> <note>The highest level of the soul in Jewish mysticism, associated with the intellect and divine awareness.</note>. Truly the living soul, greedy for dominion and glory, resides in the heart and is called <term>Ruach</term> <note>The middle level of the soul, associated with the spirit, breath, and emotional drives.</note>. That part, however, which is animal—lusting for food and drink—resides in the liver and is simply called <term>Nephesch</term> <note>The lowest level of the soul, representing the vitalizing force of the physical body and its basic instincts.</note>. Thus Plato says in his book *On the Soul of the World*: "The desiring part has its seat around the liver" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν, περὶ τὸ ἧπαρ (*to epithymētikón, peri to hēpar*)</note>; that is, the concupiscible <note>term: concupiscible. The part of the soul responsible for physical desires and appetites.</note> part of the soul is seated near the liver. In the *Timaeus*, he calls this "the soul's desire for food and drink" <note>original Greek: τὸ σίτων τε καὶ ποτῶν ἐθυμητικὸν τῆς ψυχῆς (*to sitōn te kai potōn epithymētikón tēs psychēs*)</note>; that is, that which craves drinkables and edibles. 

"The spirited part has its seat around the heart" <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ θυמוειδὲς πεרὶ τὴν καρδίαν (*to de thymoeidés peri tēn kardian*)</note>; that is, the part truly prone to anger is seated near the heart. In the *Timaeus*, he calls this "the part of the soul sharing in courage and spirit, being fond of contention" <note>original Greek: τὸ μετέχον τῆς ψυχῆς ἀνדρείας καὶ θומוῦ φιλόνעικον ὄν (*to metechon tēs psychēs andreias kai thymou philoneikon on*)</note>; that is, the part of the soul participating in fortitude and anger, and loving strife. 

"The rational part of the human soul remains established around the head" <note>original Greek: τᾶס μὲν ἀνθρωπíνας ψυχᾶס τὸ λογικὸν πεרὶ τὰν κεφαλὰν ἵדρυται μένον (*tas men anthrōpinas psychas to logikon peri tan kephalan hidrytai menon*)</note>; the part of the human soul that partakes in reason has its seat around the head. In the body, truly, the brain is the principle and root of the marrow: and in it is also the lordship of the soul. This kind of soul "God has given to each of us as a guardian spirit <note>term: dæmon. In the context of Platonic philosophy, a 'dæmon' is not an evil entity, but a personal 'genius' or the highest part of the rational soul that guides a person toward the divine.</note>; we say this spirit dwells in the highest part of our body and lifts us from the earth toward our kinship in heaven," etc., says Plato in the *Timaeus*: just as God has granted to each of us our own guardian spirit, we say this spirit has its seat in the highest fortress of the body and raises us from the earth to our heavenly kinship, as beings born from a celestial rather than a terrestrial seed. 

This is indeed quite rightly said. For from where the first origin of the soul was given, from there a divine power, fashioning the head as our root and source, raises us up and directs the whole body.

# Notes

...the most mystical of the rites. <note>original Greek: μυστικωτάτη τῶν τελετῶν (*mystikōtatē tōn teletōn*)</note>. The priests command that the entire body be buried, except for the head itself, in the most mystical part of the sacred rites.

The Kabbalists <note>term: Cabalistæ. Practitioners of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal, mysterious Infinite and the mortal, finite universe.</note> say, as it is read in the *Book of Creation* <note>term: Sefer Yetzirah. This is explained, as Rabbi Joseph son of Gikatilla <note>term: R. Ioseph filius Carnitolis. Referring to Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a prominent Spanish Kabbalist. These two levels, to which the two planets Mercury and Venus correspond, relate to the kidneys. The level of Power <note>gloss: Gevurah</note> corresponds to the heart, and the level of Understanding <note>gloss: Binah</note> to the brain. 

Thus, the sense is: if the three parts of the soul—that which is in the brain, that which is in the heart, and that which is in the kidneys—are upright and not perverted, then...

### He gathered dust from the four sides of the world.

Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Mountains of Sinai Against the Jews* <note>original: *lib. de montibus sina aduersus Iudæos*. This text is now generally attributed to a "Pseudo-Cyprian," an anonymous 3rd-century author, rather than Saint Cyprian of Carthage himself.</note>, says: "Adam received his Hebrew name from God; in Latin it is interpreted as 'earth made flesh' <note>original: *terra caro facta*. This is a folk etymology; the Hebrew name *Adam* is actually related to *adamah*, meaning 'ground' or 'earth,' and *adom*, meaning 'red.'</note>, because He grasped [the dust] from the four corners of the world in His fist, just as it is written in Isaiah 40: 'I have measured the heaven with my palm; I made man from all the mud of the earth; in the image of God I made him.'" <note>This specific phrasing does not appear in the standard Book of Isaiah; the author or his source is likely paraphrasing and combining several biblical passages to emphasize God's role as a craftsman.</note> It was fitting that Adam should bear a name derived from these four corners of the world. We find in the scriptures that the Creator of the world established four stars, one at each of the corners of the world. The first star, in the East, is called <term>Anatole: from the Greek ἀνατολὴ, meaning "rising" or "the East."</term>; the second, in the West, is <term>Dysis: from the Greek δύσις, meaning "setting" or "the West."</term>; the third star, in the North, is <term>Arktos: from the Greek ἄρκτος, meaning "the Bear"—referring to the constellation Ursa Major—or "the North."</term>; and the fourth, in the South, is <term>Mesembria: from the Greek μεσημβρία, meaning "midday" or "the South."</term> <note>The author is highlighting an ancient Christian acrostic: the first letters of these four Greek directions—**A**natole, **D**ysis, **A**rktos, **M**esembria—spell the name **ADAM**, symbolizing that the first man was composed of the entire cosmos.</note> It is said in the Talmud that God created Adam of such great size that he extended from the North to the South, and from the East to the West, as we shall discuss more extensively later.

<summary>This page explores the symbolic and etymological origins of Adam's name, citing pseudo-Cyprianic and Talmudic traditions to present Adam as a microcosm encompassing the four corners of the earth.</summary>

**Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Nevuchim*</note>, part 2, chapter 6, considers Angels to be incorporeal because they have no fixed or determined body; but like **Proteus** <note>A shape-shifting sea god from Greek mythology, used here as a metaphor for the angels' ability to change appearance.</note>, they transform themselves into various forms, such as fire, wind, men, or women.

### The end of creation is for the sake of humanity, that they may constantly serve God.

The Platonists <term>Platonists: philosophers who followed the teachings of Plato, often synthesized with Christian or Jewish theology during the Renaissance to explain how the physical world reflects divine truths.</term> say that God made the world by His goodness, out of an overflowing and immense fecundity <note>fecundity: fruitfulness or the ability to produce many offspring or ideas.</note>, which first rejoices in itself, and then, because of this, delights in this image of itself. is placed in the same order together with that which acts toward an end, and is itself a certain good that moves the driving cause. However, nothing is placed in the same order as God except **God** Himself. Therefore, if the end or goal of God is His own goodness, then **God**, in His own way, desires and loves His own goodness. He therefore wills Himself as the end of Himself and of all things; and since He made the world by His goodness, He made it for the sake of the good, and placed man within it for that same reason. For He did not create man simply so that he might exist, live, and understand in a basic sense, but so that he might exist well, live well, and understand and acquire the "good." And for this reason, God gave His law to man, so that through it he might arrive at the enjoyment of that ultimate good. This is what is meant in chapter 2: *When God intended to create the world, He looked upon the law.* <note>This refers to the Midrashic idea (found in Genesis Rabbah 1:1) that the Torah served as the architectural blueprint for the creation of the universe.</note> From this comes the interpretation through <term>notaricon: a Kabbalistic method of shorthand where the letters of a word form an acronym for a longer phrase</term> of the word *Bereshit* <note>original Hebrew: בראשית, the first word of Genesis, "In the beginning"</note>, which stands for: *In the beginning God saw that the Israelites would receive the Law.* <note>original Hebrew: בראשונה ראה אלהים שיקבלו ישראל תורה (*Berishona ra'ah Elohim she-yekablu Yisrael Torah*). Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy into a single system; here, the "maker" or Demiurge uses a divine law to order the cosmos.</note>

### On the first chapter.

...Therefore, in the book *The Juice of Pomegranates* <note>original: *Succus malorum granatorum*, referring to the work *Asis Rimmonim* by the 16th-century Kabbalist Moses Cordovero</note>: they possessed a body brought forth outside the earthly paradise, which for that reason had contracted the filth of this world; they could not, therefore, enter the Garden of Eden unless that body was first consumed. They propose a doubt to themselves: What then is the difference between those who were translated there alive, such as Elijah <note>original: *Elias*</note>, and those who are transferred after death, if it is necessary for the bodies of all who enter the earthly paradise to be first consumed? They respond: the bodies of those who die return to dust; but truly the bodies of those who are led there alive are burned and consumed by the power of the pure and holy air which is in the Garden of Eden; and there, they say, their souls put on an immortal body or garment:

<note>The following is a translation of the Hebrew text: "But he who has not tasted the taste of death: his body is finished and burned by the power of the pure and holy air which is in the Garden of Eden: and he clothes himself there in a garment without the taste of death." ### Thus all worlds form a single body.

Thus says Marsilio Ficino <note>Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated Plato into Latin and sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian theology.</note> following Plato. However many orbits we imagine scattered through the vacuum, we must conceive of just as many spheres within spheres, so that every individual sphere is a world within a world, and the entire work is a unity, ordered within itself, so that nothing is found to be either empty or lacking in order and union. 

"Having considered these things," says Plato in the *Timaeus*, "first, so that it might be as much as possible a complete living thing, perfect and consisting of perfect parts; and in addition to these, that it be one, since nothing was left over out of which another such thing might be produced." <note>original Greek: ταῦτα διανοηθεὶς... ἵνα ὅλον ὅτι μάλιστα ζῶον τέλειον ἐκ τελείων τῶν μερῶν εἴη. πρὸς δὲ τούτοις ἕν, ἅτε, οὐχ ὑπολελειμμένων ἐξ ὧν ἄλλο τοιοῦτο ἂν γένοιτο. This passage describes the Demiurge (the divine craftsman) creating the universe as a single, unique, and perfect entity.</note> That is: "And for that reason, the craftsman, having calculated the proportions—" <note>The Latin text *subductis rationi-* ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

# On Chapter Three

...dence, <note>The word fragment "dentia" likely completes "Providentia" (Providence) from the preceding page.</note> and is called Mind by Plato.

The **Jovian Mind** <note>original: "Iouia ... mens." In Neoplatonic thought, the "Jovian" or "Jupiter-like" Mind refers to the soul of the world or the Demiurge that governs the visible universe.</note> is the craftsman of all things; it is the intellect that occupies itself with visible things while it moves toward secondary matters, and it consists in the manifest production of things. It is called **Fate**, and by Plato, <term>Necessity</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀνάγκη" (anankē). In Plato's cosmology, Necessity represents the "wandering cause" or the inherent properties of matter that the divine Craftsman must persuade to achieve a good result.</note>. He speaks thus in the *Timaeus*: <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's foundational work on the origin of the physical world.</note> "For indeed, the birth of this world was mixed, being born from a combination of necessity and intellect." <note>original Greek: "μεμιγμένη γὰρ οὖν ἡ τοῦδε τοῦ κόσμου γένεσις ἐξ ἀνάγκης τε καὶ νοῦ συστάσεως ἐγενήθη."</note> That is to say, the creation of this world was a mixture; the world was brought forth from the joining of necessity and intelligence. Therefore, since the mind and intelligence of the Craftsman <note>Referring to the Demiurge, the divine figure who shapes the universe in Plato's philosophy.</note> were superior to necessity and commanded it, leading it so that as many things as possible might be brought to the best possible state; in this very way, with necessity yielding to the wise command of that Mind, this universe was established in the beginning.

However, Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, who reinterpreted Plato's works.</note> explains "necessity" and "mind" differently. For by "necessity" he understands <term>primary matter</term> <note>original: "materia prima," the formless "stuff" that underlies all physical objects.</note>, while by "mind" he understands **form**. In the *Enneads*, <note>The *Enneads* are the collected writings of Plotinus.</note> Book 1, Chapter 8, Section 7: "For indeed, the nature of this world is mixed, composed of both Mind and Necessity. And whatever comes into it from God is good; but the evils [come] from the ancient na-" <note>original Greek: "μεμιγμένη γὰρ οὖν ἡ τοῦδε τοῦ κόσμου φύσις, ἔκ τε νοῦ καὶ ἀνάγκης. καὶ ὅσα παρὰ θεοῦ εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκει, ἀγαθά: τὰ δέ κακὰ, ἐκ τῆς ἀρχαίας φύ-." The sentence breaks off at "nature" (physis).</note>

# Notes

...essity <note>This completes the word "necessity" from the previous page. The Greek text fragment "σεως" (seos) likely completes a word such as "diakosmeseos," meaning "ordering" or "arrangement."</note>, I mean the **matter**, the underlying substance, not yet ordered, if it were to be viewed in its own state. <note>original Greek: "σεως, τὴν ὕλην λέγω, τὴν ὑποκειμένην, οὔπω κοσμηθεῖσαν, εἰ θεωτοῖ."</note> That is to say: Therefore, the nature of this world is a mixture of necessity and mind.

Truly, whatever things proceed into this world from God are good; but evils proceed from the "ancient nature"—by which I mean the underlying matter not yet adorned—if it were to be perceived in that stage of its existence. For indeed, he says in Chapter 5: "That which is utterly deficient, such as matter is, is truly evil, possessing no portion of the good."

Matter truly does not possess true "being," by the gift of which it might have been able to possess "good." Instead, "being" is attributed to it only <term>equivocally</term> <note>In logic and philosophy, an equivocal term is one used with different meanings. Here, the author argues that matter does not "exist" in the same way that divine or formal things exist; its existence is a mere shadow or a different category of being.</note>, so that it can truly be said "not to exist."

The universe therefore consists, **Marsilio** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Italian scholar and priest who translated the works of Plato and Hermes Trismegistus into Latin, sparking the Renaissance interest in Neoplatonism.</note> concludes, of **Mind**—that is, the <term>formal act</term> <note>The "formal act" (actus formalis) refers to the active, shaping principle that gives a thing its specific essence and reality, as opposed to the passive potential of matter.</note>, which is surely the primary objective in the divine mind’s will and the image of that mind—and also of **Necessity**—that is, **Matter**, which is taken up for this work not so much by its own intention, but by a certain necessary condition, hiding itself under form.

## The Law, Hidden and Manifest.

"The union of the Law with the supreme Craftsman is hidden; the division according to the law is manifest," says **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Greek Neoplatonist philosopher. His "Theology of Plato" attempted to harmonize all of Greek theology into a single, logical system.</note> in *The Theology of Plato*, Book 5, Chapter 9.

"Wherefore also the Craftsman, looking toward this [Law], leads all things according to law, and establishes as an image of the union with the Father that providence which dwells within the world; but as an image of the division according to law, he establishes fate and the laws of fate." <note>original Greek: "διὸ δὴ καὶ ὁ δημιουργὸς πρὸς τοῦτον βλέπων, κατὰ νόμον ἄγει τὰ πάντα, καὶ τῆς μὲν ἑνώσεως τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς εἰκόνα τὴν ἐγκόσμιον ὑφίστησι πρόνοιαν: τῆς δὲ κατὰ τὸν νόμον διαιρέσεως τὴν εἱμαρμένην, καὶ τοὺς εἱμαρμένης νόμους."</note>

That is to say: For which reason also that **Craftsman** <note>Also known as the Demiurge, the divine figure who shapes the physical world according to a rational plan.</note> of all things, looking toward that law, acts and governs all things according to the law; and indeed, of that union with the Father himself, he established as an image that very **providence** <note>Translated from the Greek 'pronoia,' meaning divine foresight or care.</note> moving within the world (this is the **hidden path**). But of that division which occurs according to the law, [he established] **fate** <note>Translated from the Greek 'heimarmene,' referring to the fixed chain of cause-and-effect in the material realm.</note> itself, and the laws of fate themselves (this is the **manifest path**). <note>original Latin: "id est Quamobrem etiam ille rerum opifex ad istam legem spectans, omnia secundum legem agit, & regit: & illius quidem vnionis cum ipso patre imaginem constituit ipsam prouidentiam in mundo versantem (hæc est via occulta.) Illius vero diuisionis, quæ secundum legem fit, ipsum fatum, & ipsas fatales leges. (hæc est via aperta.)"</note>

In the first book, in the final chapter, he brings forward another reason why the law is called "hidden" and "manifest." He says it is manifest regarding the words, but hidden regarding that which is signified. "For each name, just like a statue of the..." <note>original Greek: "ἕκαστον γὰρ ὄνομα καθάπερ ἄγαλμα τοῦ..." This fragment suggests that words/names are like icons or images that represent a deeper, hidden reality.</note>

> "Do not defile the spirit, nor deepen the plane." <note>original Greek: μὴ πνεῦμα μολύνῃς, μηδὲ βαθύνῃς τὸ ἐπίπεδον.</note>

Nor, however, do [the Platonists] wish for the rational part of the soul to be joined directly to the vehicle; rather, the rational soul itself—insofar as it is rational and a companion of celestial souls—exerts a life-giving action upon the vehicle. They built within it another form of the soul, the mortal kind, which contains within itself terrible and necessary passions." <note>original Greek: παραλαβόντες ἀρχὴν ψυχῆς ἀθάνατον, τὸ μετὰ τοῦτο θνητὸν σῶμα αὐτοὶ περιετόρνευσαν. ὄχημά τε ἅπαν τὸ σῶμα ἔδοσαν. ἄλλό τε εἶδος ἐν αὐτῷ ψυχῆς προσωκοδόμουν τὸ θνητὸν δεινὰ καὶ ἀναγκαῖα ἐν αὐτῷ παθήματα ἔχον.</note>

That is: *They, therefore—namely the gods—having received the immortal beginning of the soul...*

# To the Fourth Chapter
->Ll iij<-

...next, they fashioned a mortal body around it and gave it the body as a **vehicle** <note>original: *vehiculum*. In Neoplatonic thought, this is the "luminous body" or astral shell that acts as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical world.</note> for the soul. Within this, they fabricated another type of soul, namely the **mortal** one (which Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the "astral vehicle" of the soul.</note> calls the **aerial vehicle**), which contains within itself heavy and necessary passions. Plato calls this soul "mortal" not because it will ever truly die, but because, as some believe, it would collapse if its vehicle were withdrawn. For just as the brightness of the Moon produces a pale glow within a cloud, so the soul in that celestial body emits an **idol** <note>original: *idolum*, from the Greek *eidolon*, meaning an image, phantom, or "double" of the self.</note>—much like a comet <note>original: *stella crinita*, literally a "maned" or "hairy star."</note> emits its tail—which would vanish if that celestial body were to vanish, just as the paleness is extinguished when the clouds are dispersed. However, because the vehicle is never truly withdrawn, Zoroaster says:

> "There is also a portion for the image in the place of surrounding light." <note>original Greek: Ἔστι καὶ εἰδώλῳ μερὶς ἐς τόπον ἀμφιφάοντα.</note>

There is a place for the **Idol** <note>The "Image" or lower aspect of the soul.</note> even in the luminous region; for it will return to heaven together with the vehicle and the rational soul. Within this idol are the senses, through which the wonderful harmonies of the heavens are often perceived, as well as the voices and bodies of **daemons** <note>original: *dæmonum*. In the classical sense, these are not "demons" but intermediary spirits or divine beings that inhabit the air and celestial spheres.</note>, whenever someone, for a time, from the earthly...

## He calls the prefect.

The Rabbis believe that angels were created at the same time as souls to take care of them, according to **Psalm 91, verse 11**: "For he has given his angels charge over you, to guard you in all your ways." <note>original Latin: *Quoniam angelis suis mandauit de te, vt custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis*</note> For this reason, they say that the angels sympathize with our misfortunes, interpreting **Isaiah chapter 57, verse 18**—"and I restored comforts to him and to those mourning him"—as it is written in the book *The Juice of Pomegranates*: <note>original Latin: *succus malorum granatorum*. This refers to the *Asis Rimmonim*, a famous 16th-century Kabbalistic work by Moses Cordovero which summarizes the teachings of the Zohar.</note>

"Because they are emanated through the emanation of his soul," <note>original Hebrew: מפני שהם יהיו נאצלים באצילות נשמתו</note> that is, because the emanation of the angels is joined with the emanation of the human soul. They assign two angels to every person, following the passage in **Deuteronomy 30, verse 15**: "I have set before you good and evil." The philosopher Empedocles <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that forces of Love and Strife govern the universe.</note> calls these "a good and an evil spirit." <note>original Greek: *καλὸν καὶ κακὸν δαίμονα* (kalon kai kakon daimona)</note> One angel is on the right, or from the level of mercy, <note>In Kabbalah, the "Right Side" is associated with *Chesed* (Loving-kindness or Mercy).</note> who rouses the person toward virtue out of love for it; the other is on the left, or from the level of fear, <note>The "Left Side" is associated with *Gevurah* (Strength, Judgment, or Fear).</note> who tests the person through various temptations. This latter one they call the angel of the "incitement to evil." <note>original Latin: *fomes mali*. This is a technical theological term for the "tinder" or inclination toward sin, corresponding to the Hebrew concept of the *Yetzer Hara*.</note>

### *That they may be delighted in seeing them, etc.*

Plato stated that God places souls into their own **vehicles** <term>vehicles: often referred to as the "astral body" or "pneumatic vehicle," this was believed by Neoplatonists to be a subtle, celestial substance that carries the soul from the heavens down into the physical body.</term> and teaches them the nature and laws of the universe. In the *Timaeus* <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's most famous dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world and the nature of the soul.</note>, he says: "Therefore, having established the whole, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars, and assigned each soul to a specific star; and having placed them there as if in the chariot of the universe, he revealed to them the laws of fate and necessity." He further showed that the first birth would be one and the same for all, so that no soul would receive less than another from Him. Once the souls were sown and scattered, as it were, it would come to pass that at certain intervals of time, a living being would be born which would be most fit for the worship of God, most religious, and most devoted to piety, and so forth.

Indeed, among the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, particularly those in the later "Neoplatonist" tradition who emphasized the soul's mystical journey.</note>, it is certain that souls are endowed with knowledge before they "slip down" into physical bodies. For they argue that if souls pre-exist, it is consistent <note>original: "consentaneum"</note> that they are filled and brimming with various branches of knowledge, and contain within themselves the **intelligible forms** <term>intelligible forms: also known as Platonic Ideas; these are the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things that exist in the material world.</term> and the underlying reasons of all things.

<summary>This page explores the Platonic theory of the soul's origin, explaining how God assigns souls to stars and "vehicles" before birth, ensuring they possess innate knowledge and a capacity for piety before entering the material world.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Timaeus, soul vehicles, pre-existence of the soul, intelligible forms, laws of fate, cosmology, Neoplatonism</keywords>

# To the Fourth Chapter.

...is [internal]. Plato proves this in the *Meno* <note>The *Meno* is a Socratic dialogue by Plato that explores the definition of virtue and whether it can be taught. It is famous for the theory of "recollection," which suggests that the soul is immortal and already contains all knowledge.</note> as follows. By questioning a boy belonging to Meno, he causes him to discover a geometrical principle along with him—not as if he were teaching it himself, he says, but only leading the way through questioning, so that the boy perceives that knowledge from within himself, evidently recalled by the guidance of the questions and the demonstration. He asks: "This knowledge, which he now possesses here—did he not either receive it at some point, or always possess it? If he always possessed it, was he not also always knowledgeable? But if he received it at some time, he certainly did not receive it in this life; for who taught this boy geometry?" He concludes: "Therefore, those ideas which a person appears not to know are actually present in the soul of that person, and they are true insights regarding those very things he seems to be ignorant of. For now, those very ideas have been awakened as if from a dream. But if someone questions him about these same matters, many times and in various ways, you may be sure that he will eventually yield to no one in his accurate and exquisite mastery of them." In the same way, the Hebrews say that the soul—even the **Ruach** <term>Ruach: A Hebrew word (רוּחַ) meaning "breath," "wind," or "spirit." Before we discuss the descent of the souls <term>souls: *Nefchamot* (Hebrew: *Neshamot*), the highest level of the human soul, representing the divine breath or intellect.</term> into the Garden of Eden and Gehenna <term>Gehenna: A place of purification or punishment for the soul after death, often equated with Purgatory or Hell in this context.</term>, and how the spirits <term>spirits: *Ruchot* (Hebrew: *Ruchot*), the intermediate level of the soul associated with emotion and ethical character.</term> are led through the whole of the Garden of Eden and Gehenna; it seems necessary for us to first provide a description of those places.

Concerning the state of souls of this kind before they glide down into bodies, Greek philosophers present something similar. The story of Er the Armenian is well known, which Plato relates in the 10th book of the *Republic* <note>original: *de Repub.* Referring to Plato’s *Republic*, book 10, which concludes with the Myth of Er, a foundational Western vision of the afterlife and reincarnation.</note>. When the souls, he says, about which we spoke above, had rested for seven days in a meadow, on the eighth day they would rise from there to travel elsewhere; and on the fourth day, they were accustomed to arrive at the designated place. From there, a light is seen from above, extended through the whole heaven and earth, like a column very similar to a rainbow, yet purer and brighter. Into that light they entered completely within the space of one day, and in the middle of the light they saw the ends of the chains extended from heaven: for that light is the bond of heaven, like the under-girding of triremes <note>original: *triremium fuccincturas*. These were heavy cables used on ancient Greek warships (triremes) to wrap around the hull and keep it together under stress; Plato uses this as a metaphor for how the light holds the universe together.</note>, and thus that light embraces the entire circumference of heaven on all sides. From the tips of the bonds, however, is suspended the Spindle of Necessity <note>original: *Neceffitatis penfum*. In the myth, this spindle determines the motions of the celestial spheres.</note>, through which all the celestial circuits are performed, etc. An adamantine spindle in...

He claimed that Lachesis assigned to each person that guiding spirit <note>original: *daemon*. A tutelary deity or personal destiny assigned to an individual for the duration of their life.</note> which they had chosen as the guardian and protector of their life, and the fulfiller of those things determined by the judgment of fate. 

This spirit then leads the soul first to the sister Clotho <note>Clotho is the "Spinner" among the three Fates, responsible for spinning the thread of human life.</note>, and under her hand and the whirling of the spindle, she confirms the fortune which had been allotted. From there, following in their footsteps, they approach the throne of Necessity. Afterwards, the guiding spirit, together with the crowd of the remaining souls, sets out in the boiling heat of a violent sun toward the Plain of Forgetfulness <note>original: *campus lethæus*. Derived from Lethe, the river or personification of oblivion in Greek mythology.</note>. ...again, what are the splendors and ornaments of **Jupiter**, if not the reasons <note>original: "rationes," which here refers to the Greek *logoi*—the divine formative principles or "blueprints" that flow from the divine mind to shape the world.</note> flowing from him? His mother is Poverty because longing belongs to those in need. Poverty is also the "matter" of Love, because matter is in need of all things. <note>original Greek: "ἐκ πόρȣ οὖν καὶ πενίας λέγεται εἶναι ἔρως: ἢ ἡ ἔλλειψις, καὶ ἡ ἔφεσις καὶ τῶν λόγων ἡ μνήμη ὁμοῦ συνελθόντα ἐν ψυχῇ ἐγέννησε τὴν ἐνέργειαν τὴν πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἔρωτα τοῦτον ὄντα. ἡ δὲ μήτηρ αὐτῷ πενία ὅτι ἂν ἡ ἔφεσις ἐνδεής. ὕλη δὲ ἡ πενία ὅτι καὶ ἡ ὕλη ἐνδεὴς τὰ πάντα." This is a quotation from Plotinus, Ennead III.5.9.</note> For this reason, Love is described as having arisen from Resource and Poverty, or from abundance and lack at the same time. Indeed, the deficiency and the yearning, joined with the memory of those divine reasons conspiring within the soul, gave birth to that movement toward the Good which is called Love. His mother is Lack, because desire always belongs to one who is in need; and the material of Love is Lack itself, because matter is destitute of everything.

Therefore, the **Platonists** assert that the soul was created without matter, which is symbolized by **Poverty** being outside the doors during the birthday banquet of **Venus**. However, they describe the soul’s reason and its appetite—that is, **Resource** drunk on nectar, or the power passing into action—as being in the gardens of **Jupiter**; that is, the soul is endowed with the memory of the reasons emanating from God,

# On the fifth chapter.

Rr

...joined with **Poverty**—that is, with matter—to produce an act directed toward the Good, which is called **Love**. Just as the **Jews** say that the *Neshamah* <note>original Hebrew: *Neshamah*. In Jewish mystical tradition, this is the intellectual or divine soul, the highest of the three parts of the human spirit.</note>, the intellectual soul, before it falls into the body, descends into the **Garden of Eden**; there, along with its own form, it produces an act directed toward either good or evil.

### After she descends into the world, the King crowns her with seven Crowns.

In this way, the **Platonists** assign the boundaries of seven numbers to the soul, which is represented by the figure of a triangle. Truly, since we see that the generation of all things is governed by the seven-fold number of the **Planets**, and that **Saturn**, the highest of the planets, causes transitions in human life every seventh year, and the **Moon**, the lowest of the planets, brings about changes every seventh day—both within herself and in the bodily humors <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the "humors" were the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to regulate health and temperament based on planetary influence.</note>—it is with good reason that they attribute the seven-fold number to the soul, which is the very origin of motion and generation...

<note>The soul is often described as a triangle in Platonic thought because it is the first "surface" or "plane" of existence, following the point and the line, representing its ability to bridge the divine and the material.</note>
