The Rabbis reconcile all those aforementioned sayings by stating that the dead do not rise according to the common order of nature, but by a miracle. And thus Rabbi Meir al-Dabi <note>Rabbi Meir ben Isaac al-Dabi (14th century) was a Spanish Jewish scholar known for his work *Sefer Shevilei Emunah* (The Paths of Faith), which covers philosophy, theology, and science.</note> elegantly says in the book *The Paths of Faith*:

There is no difference between the saying, "If a man dies, shall he live again?" <note>Job 14:14</note> and the saying, "Shall we bring forth water for you from this rock?" <note>Numbers 20:10</note>. For neither is within the power of nature, but is rather impossible according to it. However, water did indeed come out of that rock through a wonder; so too the resurrection of the dead is truly among the wonders. <note>original Hebrew: "אין הפרש בין אמרו אם ימות גבר היחיה: או אמרו המן הסלע הזה נוציא לכם מים שאין זה בטבע אבל נמנע בו : אלא שכבר יצאו המים מן הסלע ההוא במופת : כן תחיית המתים אולם הוא מן המופתים."</note>

That is to say, there is no distinction between this saying of Job—*Do you think a dead man shall live again?*—and this from Numbers chapter 20, verse 10: *Shall we be able to bring water out of this rock for you?* For both are beyond nature, and according to nature, they are impossible. But the fact that water once flowed from the rock was done by a miracle; so also the resurrection of the dead is surely miraculous. 

It is miraculous on the part of the body, which was first formed in the mother’s womb; since it is later consumed by death, how could it ever be restored by the forces of nature, especially outside the mother's womb? However, on the part of the soul, it can be considered natural—that is, provided the same body is restored to its wholeness. Since the soul... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

## To the Seventh Chapter.
<center>Vu ij</center>

I, for my part, when I hear this—that God is present to some spontaneously, whether through the cycle of birth or through other causes—find it laughable. For that which is unbegotten would no longer be the superior being if the cycle of birth were to lead it; nor would He be the First Cause of all things if, because of other causes, He were ranked alongside certain people. These ideas are unworthy of the favor we receive from the gods and are alien to the works performed in theurgy. <note>original Greek: ἐγώ γε καὶ τοῦτο ἀκούων... This passage is likely from Iamblichus’s *De Mysteriis* (On the Mysteries), a foundational text for Renaissance scholars interested in how humans communicate with the divine.</note> 

That is: I laugh when I hear such things: that God is present to some by a kind of chance, and as if "from a machine," <note>original Latin: *quasi ex machina*. This refers to the ancient theatrical practice of lowering a god onto the stage to solve a problem, here used to mock the idea of a "mechanical" God who appears just because the stars are aligned.</note> through the power of a celestial figure in one's birth chart, or because of other causes. For neither would that which is unbegotten be the most excellent, nor the First Cause of all, if He were made a slave to someone through the cycle of generation <term>generation: the process of being born into the physical, material world</term> and through external causes. These notions are therefore unworthy of the thoughts we should hold concerning the Gods, and are alien to those things which take place in **Theurgy** <term>Theurgy: from the Greek *theourgia*, meaning "god-work." Unlike mere prayer, it involves rituals intended to unite the practitioner with divine energies.</term>. 

(In which <note>original Greek: παρὰ μόνων Θεῶν ἡ τῶν θείων ἔργων ἐνδίδοται κατόρθωσις... </note> the success of divine works is granted by the Gods alone; for there would be no need at all for our worship if divine blessings were already available to us by our own power.) 

That is: Divinity itself is the sole cause of divine works; otherwise, religious practice would not be necessary for us to attain these things, if we were capable of possessing the Good without the worship of the gods—

*BM* <note>original Hebrew: בם (Bet-Mem). In the context of Psalm 68:17, "The Lord is among them [bam] at Sinai," Kabbalists interpret the word "among them" as a mystical name.</note> in Sinai, that is God, whose name is *BM* derived from 42 letters. <note>The Name of 42 Letters is a legendary Kabbalistic name of God, often associated with the prayer *Ana B'Koach*.</note> Furthermore, *Bet* (ב) is the beginning of Genesis <note>The first letter of the first word of the Bible, *Bereshit*, is *Bet*.</note> and *Mem* (ם) is the end; <note>The final letter of many Hebrew words and the conclusion of certain creative cycles.</note> it is as if the Psalmist wished to say: The Lord, the author of creation, was present at Sinai.

### Regarding the name of 72 letters.

They also derive the name of 72 letters from the name of four letters <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</term> by taking the *Yod* (י) separately, which equals 10; then *Yod-He* (יה), which is 15; then *Yod-He-Vav* (יהו), which is 21; and finally *Yod-He-Vav-He* (יהוה), which is 26. By adding all of these together, the total is 72. <note>10 + 15 + 21 + 26 = 72. This pyramidal calculation is a standard technique in Gematria.</note> Others derive it from the holy name when written out in its full "filled" form: *Yod-Vav-Dalet*, *He-Yod*, *Vav-Yod-Vav*, *He-Yod*. <note>original Hebrew: יוד הי ויו הי. This specific expansion, where the letters are spelled out to total 72, is known as *Ab*.</note>

### Regarding the name of 12 letters.

Indeed, they form the name of twelve letters in various ways. Some do so by the addition of the two letters *Aleph-He* (אה) and *Aleph-He* (אה). Others derive it from the letter *Vav* (ו) when it is written as *Vav-Vav* (וו). Still others form it by multiplying the 4 letters of the Tetragrammaton (יהוה) by the three different letters that compose it (*Yod*, *He*, and *Vav*); for indeed, three times four produce 12.

## Regarding the name of 4 letters.

The origin of all these names is the four-letter name <term>YHWH: The Tetragrammaton, the most holy name of God in the Hebrew Bible.</term>, which they call "the square name." This is because, as Rabbi Meir al-Dabi <note>original: "R. Mekir Aldabi." Meir ben Isaac al-Dabi (14th century) was a Spanish Jewish scholar and author of *Shevilim di-Yehudah*.</note> says, the letters of that name "preserve themselves in number" <note>original Hebrew: שומרות עצמם במספר (*shomerot atzmam b'mispar*)</note>. This means that when squared, their final digit remains the same: 

For 10 times 10 produces 100. Behold, 10 always remains. <note>In the system of Hebrew numerals, *Yod* is 10. While 10 squared is 100 (*Kuf*), in certain numerological systems, the base essence of the 10 is seen as recurring or being preserved within the structure of 100.</note> 

*He* (ה) *He* (ה): 5 times 5 is 25. Behold, 5 remains. <note>The letter *He* represents 5; its square ends in 5.</note> 

*Vav* (ו) *Vav* (ו): 6 times 6 is 36. 6 always remains. <note>The letter *Vav* represents 6; its square ends in 6.</note> 

"And this points toward the unity" <note>original Hebrew: וזה יורה על היחוד (*ve-zeh yoreh al ha-yichud*)</note>—that is, this mathematical property demonstrates the oneness of that name and of the One it signifies.

Add the following from the author of *The Examination of the World* <note>original Latin: *Examinis mundi*. This refers to the *Bechinat Olam*, a famous ethical and philosophical poem by Jedaiah ben Abraham Bedersi (c. 1270–1340).</note>:

I am young in days, and they are aged;
I am more ignorant than any man, and they are wiser than the wise.
Before I was stored in the womb, the siege-mounds were poured out to shut me in; <note>The poet uses the metaphor of a besieged city to describe the soul's entry into the physical body.</note>
Before I was created, the snares were set to trap me;
And before I emerged from the womb, they seized the crossings to capture me.
They crossed the dust, they called to me, and their right hand struck me;
But this was according to the necessity of the celestial arrangement. <note>This likely refers to the astrological or providential "necessity" of the soul's descent into the material world.</note>

### *The souls of the other nations are derived from the Active Intellect.*

The Peripatetic school <term>Peripatetic: The followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkways where they held their discussions</term> divides the Intellect into the Active and the Passive. The Active Intellect <term>Active Intellect: In Aristotelian thought, the eternal, immortal part of the mind that transforms sensory information into abstract knowledge</term> is the most important part of the soul; Aristotle calls it the "difference" <note>Aristotle uses the term "differentia" to define what makes a soul uniquely human—namely, reason.</note> of the soul in Book 3 of *On the Soul*, chapter 5. It is the rational principle of the soul.

[ratio]nal <note>The text begins with "-nali," the suffix of "rationali" (rational), continuing from the previous page's discussion of the rational soul.</note> like a disposition <term>disposition: Latin *habitus*, referring to a stable state or a developed capacity of the mind</term>, through which the soul itself draws out from potentiality those things that can be understood, and makes them actually understood. For since things that are potentially understood <note>original: *Intelligibilia*</note> are material, they cannot become actually understood unless they are stripped of their matter—that is, through abstraction <term>abstraction: the mental process of "drawing out" a universal concept from a physical object by ignoring its material qualities</term>. Such things cannot be produced by a power that uses a material organ for its work, or one that is itself material, since nothing acts beyond its own inherent strength. Therefore, the thinking soul is the only one that can do this, as it is unmixed <note>original: *immixta*. In Aristotelian philosophy, this means the intellect is not "mixed" with a physical body or organ.</note> and does not use a physical organ in performing its function.

So said Aristotle in Book 3 of *On the Soul*, chapter 5: And such an intellect is of one kind by becoming all things, and of another by making all things, like a sort of disposition. <note>original Greek: *καὶ ἔστιν ὁ μὲν τοιοῦτος νοῦς τῷ πάντα γίνεσθαι: ὁ δὲ τῷ πάντα ποιεῖν ὡς ἕξις τις*. Aristotle is distinguishing between the "passive" intellect, which receives information, and the "active" intellect, which processes it.</note> That is to say: "And a certain intellect is such that it becomes all things, and another is such that it acts upon and produces all things, like a certain disposition."

Hence, in the school of the Arabs, Al-Ghazali <note>Algazel: The Latinized name of Abu Hamid Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a major Persian theologian and philosopher whose works were influential in Medieval Europe.</note> says in Book 2, Treatise 5, Chapter 2, that the soul indicates the existence of the Active Intellect <term>Active Intellect: the force that enables the human mind to transition from having the *capacity* to learn to actually *knowing* universal truths</term>. For the human soul is a knower of abstract concepts and universal intentions <term>universal intentions: general mental concepts, like "humanity," rather than specific individuals like "Socrates"</term> at the start of childhood, but only in potentiality. Afterwards, however, it becomes a knower in actuality. But everything that moves from potentiality to [actuality...] <note>The sentence concludes on the following page.</note>

[...into] actuality, it requires a cause by which it is drawn toward actuality. ...active principle, rather than a passive one. It is no obstacle that from the beginning of our birth, the Intellect is not present within us in a perfect state, since, existing in the body as its <term>act: the "actualizing principle" or the thing that gives the body its specific function and life</term>, it can by no means be perfect from the start. Instead, it is made perfect through use, because it requires the senses and the <term>phantasia: the faculty of imagination or the ability to form mental images from sensory input</term>, which are strengthened and perfected along with the physical body. 

And for that reason, as long as the Intellect dwells in the body, it is necessary for it to understand <term>Universals: general concepts or essences, like "triangularity" or "humanity," that apply to many things at once</term>—which the Intellect itself has separated through its own workmanship from matter and the conditions of matter—by means of <term>phantasmata: mental images derived from sensory experiences</term> and within individual, specific things. 

Thus, to understand universals in a universal way, without the limitations of matter, proves that the Intellect is <term>separable and unmixed: independent from physical matter and not blended with the body's substance</term>. However, to understand these same universals within individual objects proves that the Intellect is currently situated in matter and hindered by it. 

Nevertheless, because we do not reason immediately from infancy, some thinkers have posited that the principle of understanding—that is, the <term>Active Intellect: the "Intellectus agens," the power that illuminates the mind to allow for abstract thought</term>—is something external to us. Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>original: "Alexander Aphrodisæus"; a celebrated commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) who argued that the human mind is mortal, while the "Active Intellect" that allows us to think is actually God himself.</note> established that this is God, the Best and Greatest, who is the first cause of all things and the first being, upon whom all beings depend for their existence...

### The Soul of the Israelites truly emanates from a holy place.

Just as the Rabbis <term>Rabbini: Jewish scholars and teachers of the law</term> attribute a created beginning to the souls of the nations <term>gentium: refers here to non-Jewish people or Gentiles</term>, so they say that the souls of the Israelites emanate from an uncreated principle. That is to say, they come from a holy place, from a pure and holy cause, from the throne of glory—in a word, they proceed immediately from God, just as light comes from light, or as a lamp is lit from a fire. Thus, God is called "Fire" in Deuteronomy 4:24: *The Lord your God is a consuming fire* <note>original: "Dominus Deus tuus Ignis consumens est"</note>; and the soul is called a "lamp" in Proverbs 20:27 <note>The OCR reads chapter 2, but the biblical verse cited is Proverbs 20:27</note>: *The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord* <note>original: "lucerna Dei anima hominis"</note>. From this, the soul is called *Neshamah* <term>Neschamah: one of the Hebrew terms for the soul, specifically the higher, divine breath of life</term>, as if it were *breathed into the light* <note>original: "מתנשמת באור" (mitnashmet ba-or)</note>, that is, inspired into the air.

### *That the soul is an absolute substance subsisting by itself.*

<note>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral and vine motifs.</note>

That the <term>Intellectual Soul: the highest faculty of the human soul, responsible for reason and the comprehension of abstract truths</term> is an absolute <term>substance: in classical philosophy, an entity that exists in its own right and does not depend on another thing for its existence</term> subsisting through itself and separate from matter is a certainty among the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato, who argued that the soul is immortal and exists independently of the physical body.</note>, who assert that it was created before the body. ...[it follows that the intellect] knows individual things universally without the conditions of matter. This does not apply to the senses, which do not perceive objects entirely without some condition of matter, because they know those things only as singular individuals. Furthermore, the intellect knows all things, both material and immaterial—such as when it contemplates itself and perceives that it is poorly situated or hindered within the body. Yet the senses do not even perceive all material things, such as <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical reality</term> and mathematical points; the intellect, therefore, knows these without <term>species: mental representations or "forms" through which the mind perceives objects</term>. The same is true for privations <note>original: *privationes*; the absence of a quality that should be present, such as darkness being the absence of light</note>, which it understands through their opposite positive state. 

Hence Aristotle, in Book 1 of *On the Soul*, chapter 3, as interpreted by <term>St. Thomas: Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian who synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian thought</term>, proves that because the mind knows all things—the <term>indivisible: things that cannot be broken into parts, like points or abstract concepts</term> as well as the <term>divisible: physical things that have parts and extension in space</term>—it must itself be indivisible. For if we assume the intellect is indivisible, the reason why it understands both the divisible and the indivisible becomes easily apparent: it understands the indivisible according to the property of its own nature (which is indivisible), while it understands the divisible by <term>abstracting: the mental process of "drawing out" a universal concept from a specific, physical example</term> from that which is divisible. If, however, the Intellect is established as divisible,

Finally, it is established that in <term>ecstasy: from the Greek *ekstasis*, meaning "to stand outside oneself"; a state where the mind or spirit appears to operate independently of the physical body</term> people are able to exercise the operation of the mind and will for a long time without any service of the body, and without any aid of the <term>imagination: in the original Latin *phantasia*, this refers to the mental faculty that processes sensory images</term>. He claims this happens because the soul, when released and resting from its own physical movements, perceives external and remote things. This would not occur unless the soul knew things more sharply once the body’s hindrances were removed. And yet, in this "excess of the mind" or ecstasy, the body is still affected, which is why Aristotle called it a disease in his book *On Dreams* <note>original: *de Insomniis*</note>. Furthermore, the <term>intellective: the higher power of the mind capable of abstract thought</term> faculty is further removed from the imagination than the imagination is from the external senses, because the latter two are both <term>sensitive faculties: powers of the soul that rely on physical organs and sensory input</term>. Since, however, the imagination can exist without the external senses, why should the intellect not be able to exist without the imagination? For indeed, if the mind were mixed with the body, it would either exist as a "quality"—and thus it could be hot, or cold, and so on—or it would exist as a "form," and thus it would possess a physical organ just like a sensitive power. This is because things that cannot exist without a body cannot operate without a body: and thus

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from page 366 regarding the nature of the intellect. The previous page ended while discussing why the intellect must be distinct from physical senses; this page concludes that the intellect cannot have a physical organ because it would be overwhelmed by powerful concepts and would be limited in its scope, much like a physical eye is limited to seeing only light and color.</meta>

<page-num>367</page-num>
<header>on the eighth chapter.</header>

...it would know [things] individually, and it would be corrupted by an intense <term>intelligible: an object of pure thought or an abstract concept, as opposed to a physical object</term>, just as a sense is corrupted by an intense <term>sensible: something that can be perceived by the physical senses, like a very bright light or a very loud sound</term>. For if the intellect possessed a physical organ, it would be defined by the ratio and proportion of that organ, which is undoubtedly liable to be destroyed by a violent stimulus—just as the harmony, or the ratio of high and low notes in stringed instruments, is ruined when the strings are struck too forcefully. 

But, as <term>Plotinus: a major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who explored the relationship between the soul and the divine</term> says in his *Enneads* <note>original: *Ennead.* 4. lib. 7. cap. 8.</note>: "If to feel is for the soul, while using the body, to perceive sensible things, then to Understand will not be to apprehend through the body; otherwise, Understanding and sensing would be the same thing." 

Add to this that if the soul used a physical organ to understand, it would then require another organ to understand that first organ, and so on to infinity <note>This is a classic "infinite regress" argument: if every act of knowing required a physical tool, you would need a tool to monitor the tool, never reaching a final point of understanding.</note>. 

Furthermore, if it used one specific part of the body as its organ (for no one would say it uses the entire body as an organ, since we observe that when one part of the body is <term>mutilated: injured or lost</term>, the operations of the soul occur no less effectively), it would not be able to understand all things, just as all sensible objects do not fall under the range of a single sense <note>For instance, the eye can only perceive color and light, not sound or smell. If the intellect were a physical organ like the eye, it would be limited to one "type" of thought rather than being able to grasp all universal truths.</note>. 

Finally, if there were any organ of the intellect, it would be the brain; yet who could say this, since it is not otherwise organized

<summary>This page argues that the human intellect cannot be a physical organ of the body. It uses the logic that while physical senses can be overwhelmed by strong stimuli (like being blinded by the sun), the intellect grows stronger with complex ideas, proving its non-physical nature.</summary>

Because the nature of the spirits is to be clear and bright when a person is in good health, they become darkened and clouded. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul (the transcription begins with the end of the word "animam") and its relationship to the body, specifically drawing on Neoplatonic philosophy to argue for the soul's independence and immaterial nature.</meta>

...the **soul** <term>anima: the vital principle or "breath" that gives life to a body</term> insofar as it understands is separate from the body, unmixed, and **impassible** <term>impassibilis: incapable of being acted upon, harmed, or changed by external physical forces</term>, even if it is united to **matter** <term>materia: the physical substance of the world</term> in its role as the principle of life. This is the view found in Plotinus, *Enneads*, Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 22: "Should we not say that the soul, in its act of understanding, is in the body just as fire—that is, light—is in the air? For while light is present to the air, it is not 'present' [in a physical, mingling sense]; and though it is present throughout the whole, it is mixed with nothing. The light remains itself, while the air flows through it."

For this reason, he says, it is correct to say: *as the air is in the light, rather than the light in the air* <note>original Greek: ὡς ὁ ἀὴρ ἐν τῷ φωτὶ; ἤπερ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῷ ἀέρι</note>. That is, the air is contained within the light, rather than the light being contained within the air. Therefore, Plato, in his account of the world’s creation, did not wish to say that the Soul was placed within the body, but rather that the body was positioned within the Soul. He says there is a certain part of the soul in which no body exists; this refers to those powers of the soul for which the body is not required at all.

*And in Enneads, Book 1, Chapter 8:* This indicates that the soul is not united to matter. It is shown again by the fact that *one single thing does not arise from the soul and matter together* <note>original Greek: τὸ μὴ ἔν τι ἐξ αὐτῆς καὶ ὕλης γενέσθαι</note>; a single entity is not formed from the soul and matter joined. Finally, this suggests that the soul is not in matter as if in a **subject** <term>subiectum: in classical philosophy, the underlying "thing" that holds properties, like how a piece of wood is the subject that "holds" the color brown</term>.

## From whence evil first arose for the soul.

As Socrates recounts from the words of Cebes in Plato’s *Phaedo*, the very fact that the soul entered the human body marked the beginning of its ruin. It was like a disease, causing the soul to live this life in constant torment from the weight of its misfortunes, until at last it meets its end in that which we call **death**. In this view—that the soul perishes due to the defects of the body—Cebes is rebuked by Socrates. Socrates provides many arguments to demonstrate that the soul is, in fact, **immortal**.

It is indeed true that the human soul is immortal in its own substance, and its primary function—namely **intellection** <note>original: *Intelligere*. This refers to the highest form of rational thought, which the author argues can exist independently of physical senses.</note>—is separable from the body. However, nothing prevents the soul from being considered mortal in regard to certain other faculties and operations. Specifically, these are the **vegetative** <note>The most basic level of life-functions, such as growth and nutrition.</note> and **sensitive** <note>Functions related to sensory perception and physical movement.</note> faculties. These are shared by both the soul and the physical body; they necessarily require a body to function, and on account of...

### *That the soul which remains after death is not the soul that existed when man was first made.*

So it is that the former soul perishes like a kind of harmony; <note>The "harmony" theory suggests that the soul is not a distinct substance, but rather a balanced state of the physical body's elements.</note> this is the argument that Simmias proposes to Socrates in Plato's *Phaedo*. <note>The *Phaedo* is one of Plato's most famous dialogues, set during the final hours of Socrates' life, focusing on the immortality of the soul.</note> "If therefore the soul," he says, "is a kind of harmony, then surely when our body has been excessively loosened or stretched by diseases or other evils, it is then plainly necessary that the soul perish, just as other harmonies do, which are [found in music or crafts]..."

The intellectual soul, before its composition within the body, is like a king sitting in his palace. Its composition within the body is like a king bound in the troughs <note>The Hebrew *rehatim* refers to conduits or troughs; the Latin translator here interprets this as being bound to a "beam."</note>, and its separation from the body is like a prisoner who has gone out from the house of prisoners and returned to his kingdom.

That is: The intellectual soul <note>original: *anima intellectiua*. In medieval philosophy, this is the highest part of the human soul, responsible for reason and spiritual perception.</note>, before it is joined to the body, is like a King sitting in his palace; once joined to the body, it is like a King bound to a beam; but when separated from the body, it is like one who, having gone out from prison, has recovered his kingdom. And in this way he explains that passage from Ecclesiastes 4:2: "And I praised the dead more than the living," and I judge more fortunate than both the one who has not yet been born.

<meta>This page transitions from the medieval Jewish philosophical perspectives of the previous page to Classical Greek views on the relationship between the body and the soul. It continues the "Notes" section, focusing on the etymological and philosophical origins of why the body is considered a prison or tomb for the soul.</meta>

<page-num>379</page-num>
<header>Regarding Chapter Nine.</header>
<sig>Bbb ij</sig>

Plato, in his dialogue *Cratylus*, says: Some claim that the body <note>original: *Σῶμα* (*sōma*)</note> is the tomb <note>original: *σῆμα* (*sēma*)</note> of the soul—that is, the body is the soul’s sepulcher, as if the soul were buried in the body during this present time. However, it seems to me most correct that Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek poet and prophet; the "Orphic" mysteries taught that the soul was divine and imprisoned in the physical body as punishment for ancient sins.</note> and his followers noted the origin of this word to signify that the soul is paying a penalty, and to explain the reason why it must pay it. Therefore, the soul carries this body around like an enclosure or a barrier—the very image of a prison—so that it might be <term>saved<gloss>original: *σώζηται* (*sōzētai*)</gloss></term>, which is to say, preserved. And thus, the body is for the soul exactly what its name suggests, until the soul has fully paid its debts while in the body. Indeed, it is called the <term>soma<gloss>body</gloss></term>—without changing even a single letter—because it is derived from the word for <term>being saved<gloss>original: *σώζεσθαι* (*sōzesthai*)</gloss></term> <note>Plato is engaging in wordplay here, suggesting the body is a "keep" or "safe" where the soul is held securely until its sentence is served.</note>.

But Father Jupiter, says Plotinus in the *Enneads* <note>Book 4, treatise 3, chapter 12. Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, having pitied the suffering souls, fashioned for them the bonds by which they are distressed so that they might be dissolvable <note>original: *solubilia*. Plotinus suggests that while the body is a prison, the Creator made it temporary and mortal as an act of mercy, allowing the soul eventually to be released.</note>.

### He set his steps on the path to a remote land.

Plotinus eloquently describes this in the *Enneads*, Book 3, Tractate 4, Chapter 6:

Therefore, the soul first enters this universe together with this <term>guardian spirit<gloss>original: *dæmone*</gloss></term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the *daemon* is not an evil being but a guiding spirit or higher consciousness that accompanies the soul through its life cycles.</note>, as if into a skiff. Next, the nature of that which is called by Plato the <term>cosmic spindle<gloss>original: *susus [fusus] mundanus*</gloss></term> <note>A reference to the "Spindle of Necessity" from the Myth of Er in Plato’s *Republic*, which represents the mechanisms of the universe and the spinning of individual fates.</note> and the spindle of destiny, taking up the soul as if it were in a ship, places it in a certain order upon a particular seat of fortune. 

As the cosmic revolution—like a wind—carries the soul around while it sits or even walks about in the ship, many and various spectacles occur, as well as transformations and accidents. This happens just as it does in a physical ship, whether through the tossing of the vessel itself, or from the internal impulse of the passenger who is being moved, which arises because the soul behaves in a way that exceeds its own nature while on board; for not everyone is shaken, or wills, or acts in the same way under the same circumstances. <note>original: "γίνεται οὖν διάφορα διαφόροις ἢ ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν, ἢ διαφόρων προσπεσόντων; ἢ τὰ αὐτὰ ἄλλοις, κἂν διάφορα τὰ..."</note> Therefore, different outcomes occur for different individuals, whether from the same events or from different events befalling them; or the same things happen to others, even if the circumstances are different...

...all created already before, since the prophet said: "I have made," in the past tense <note>The author refers to the grammatical tense of the Hebrew in Isaiah 57:16 as proof that the creation of souls was a completed act in the distant past.</note>. Plato defends this same opinion in the *Epinomis* <note>The *Epinomis* is a philosophical dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato, acting as a sequel to the *Laws*; it discusses the study of the stars and the divine nature of the soul.</note>.

For that which is better is also more ancient and more divine; and therefore it is more likely that the better thing exists before that which is worse, younger, and more ignoble. By this same reasoning, that which commands possesses the authority and power of rule over that which obeys and is subject to it; and the leader is entirely more ancient than the one who is led. Let us therefore take this as our starting point: that the soul is more ancient than the body. 

"So that the things of the soul," as he says in the tenth book of the *Laws* <note>original Greek: ὥστε καὶ τὰ ψυχῆς... τῶν τοῦ σώματος ἔσοιτο πρεσβύτερα. That is to say, it is equally established that those qualities belonging to the soul are prior to those things suited to the physical body. Therefore, character, emotions <note>original: *affectus*. These are the "passions" or "affections" of the mind, such as love, anger, or desire.</note>, acts of will, thoughts, true opinions, diligence, and memory—all these were created before the physical dimensions of length, breadth, depth, and strength, just as the soul itself was created before the body.

**"And she was the bride of Moses"** <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-ihi havat kallat Mosheh* (ואיהי הות כלת משה).</note>: and this was the bride of Moses, who is joined to Aaron in the degree of Majesty <note>original Latin: *Majestas*. **"Know and understand that this attribute, the Bride, is called in all places the Oral Law..."** <note>This section translates the Hebrew passage beginning *Ve-da ve-havan* (ודע והבן).</note> That is: Know and understand that this property is called the **Bride** and is referred to in all places as the <term>Oral Law</term> <note>The traditional interpretations and legal rulings transmitted verbally, as opposed to the Five Books of Moses.</note>, because she is the spouse of the <term>Written Law</term> <note>The Torah as it is written in the scroll.</note>. For this reason, she is called the **Moon** by those skilled in the mystery. The reasoning is the same for both: just as the Moon has no light of its own but receives it from the sun, so also the Oral Law has no foundation except from the Written Law. For this reason, the Oral Law was not given at Mount Sinai in writing; this was to avoid establishing a fixed place for it except upon the Written Law, because of the "secret of the Kiss." And this is the secret reason behind the verse: *Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.* <note>Song of Solomon 1:2. In Kabbalistic thought, the "kiss" represents the spiritual union and the transfer of divine breath or word between the Written and Oral traditions.</note>

...to that God, whose servants and ministers they are, they will soon arrive. But humans, because they themselves dread death, also invent lies against the **swans** <note>original: *cygnos*</note>; they claim that the birds sing out of grief, lamenting their death with a song more intense because of their pain. Yet they fail to notice that no bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or afflicted by any other kind of pain—not even the **Nightingale** <term>Luscinia: a bird often associated in Greek myth with the tragic story of Philomela</term>, nor the **swallow** <term>hirundo</term>, nor the **Hoopoe** <term>Upupa</term>, all of which are said to sing out of sorrow. 

But it does not seem to me that even these birds, nor the swans themselves, sing because of pain. Rather, I believe it is because the swans are dedicated to **Apollo** <note>Apollo was the Greek god of music, truth, and prophecy; swans were one of his sacred animals.</note>, and are thus endowed with a certain **prophetic instinct** <term>diuinandi instinctus</term>. Because they foresee the good things that exist in the **underworld** <note>original: *inferos*; refers to the realm of the dead, which Socrates views here as a place of divine reward</note>, they sing and are more delighted on that day of their death than at any previous time in their lives. 

Truly, I consider myself to be joined in the fellowship of the same service with the swans, and to be sacred to that same God; I have not received a lesser faculty of prophecy from that Lord than they have, nor do I depart from this life with a more troubled spirit.

However, the fact that it is not granted to us to foreknow our death is due to the condition of **our nature**...

...should be attributed to our condition: for we would either foresee death with all its circumstances as something **contingent** <note>original: *contingentem*; in philosophy, a "contingent" event is one that happens by chance or choice and is not strictly inevitable.</note>, or as something **necessary**. It would not be contingent: for we would either know it was coming so that we might avoid it—and in that case, how would death be "foreknown" to us, since it would never actually happen? Or we would know it was coming so that, even though it could be avoided, we would nevertheless not avoid it. 

That, however, would be the result of either great imprudence—which does not befit **wise men** <note>original: *sapientes*</note>—or of a weariness of this life, which happens to only a few. Or perhaps it would be due to a state of helplessness, which would be a companion to our misery; thus, having death constantly placed before our eyes, it would torture us with perpetual grief. It remains, therefore, to be said that we would foresee death as something that must necessarily happen in the future. 

But truly, would that be a violent death? Or one according to the common necessity of nature? Not a violent one—for example, that a person was to be killed by another. For in that case, there would be no place for **free will** <term>liberum arbitrium: the philosophical concept that humans have the power to make choices that are not determined by prior causes or divine fate</term>, since neither the person who foresaw himself becoming a **killer** <note>original: *occisorem*</note> could govern his own actions, nor could the person who knew beforehand he would be killed by another escape that person's hand, or...

### That the soul which first emanated from on high is the very same soul that survives after death.

To those who deny that the **soul** <term>anima: the vital principle or spirit of a human being</term> survives after death, the same thing seems to happen as occurs to those who look upon **Glaucus of the sea** <note>In Greek mythology, Glaucus was a fisherman who became an immortal sea-god; over time, his body became so encrusted with shells and seaweed that he no longer looked human. In the same way, while they see the soul distracted and surrounded by earthly passions and habits, they believe they are contemplating something earthly rather than something heavenly. "Shall we," he says, "propose two types of things: one that is **Visible** <note>original Latin: *Confpicabilis*</note> and another that is **Invisible** <note>original Latin: *Inconfpicabilis*</note>?" "Let us so propose," says **Cebes** <note>A philosopher from Thebes and a student of Socrates who appears as a primary interlocutor in the *Phaedo*.</note>, "and let the Invisible be that which is always the same, immortal and divine; and let the Visible be that which is never the same." Now then, are we composed of anything other than body and soul? To which type shall we decide the body is more similar and more closely related? "To anyone," he says, "it is clear: it is similar to the Visible, human, mortal, lacking in intelligence, multiform, and dissoluble type, which is never the same. But the soul is similar to the divine, Invisible model—to the **Intelligible** <term>Intelligibili: that which can only be perceived by the mind or intellect, rather than the physical senses</term>, uniform, and indissoluble—and to that which remains similarly and in the same manner..."

### On the Eleventh Chapter.

...the **soul** is most similar to the divine. For when the **soul** <term>ψυχὴ (psychē): the vital breath or spiritual essence of a person</term> considers things by itself, it departs toward that which is pure, ever-existing, and immortal, and remains in that same state. Being kindred to that realm, the soul always dwells with it, whenever it is alone by itself and has the power to do so. <note>This is a direct quote from Plato's *Phaedo* 79d. Socrates argues that when the soul uses the body to perceive, it gets confused, but when it contemplates alone, it reaches the unchanging truth.</note> 

The soul itself contemplates through itself and hastens toward that destination—namely, to that which is pure, and which always exists, and is immortal, and which remains the same. <note>original: *Anima ipsa per se ipsam contemplatur...* This is the author’s Latin translation of the preceding Greek quote from Plato.</note> Since it is kindred to this realm, it is always occupied with it, whenever it is within itself and has the power. Since this is the case, is it not characteristic and peculiar to the **body** that it should be quickly dissolved, but characteristic of the **soul** that it should remain indissoluble, or something very near to it? 

Indeed. For you see that when a man dies, the visible body—placed in the visible world, which we call the dead body or corpse, and which is naturally suited to be dissolved, to fall away, and to be breathed out <note>original: *efflari*, a term suggesting the dissipation of the spirit or the physical "breath" of life leaving the remains</note>—does not immediately suffer any of these things. Instead, it remains for a considerable time, especially if the person treated their body with a certain refinement and moderation right up until their passing. For where the dead body has fallen—

Socrates refers to Egyptian mummification to argue that if even a preserved physical body can last for centuries, the immortal soul must be far more durable.</note>, it remains almost entirely intact for a long and nearly infinite time. And even if some members of the body should decay, the bones, nerves, and all such things nevertheless endure, so to speak, as if they were immortal. Is this not so? Certainly.

The **Soul** <note>original: *Animus*. While *anima* often refers to the life-breath, *animus* here emphasizes the rational soul or mind.</note>, however—that invisible thing—surely departs to another place of that same kind: noble, pure, and invisible, truly toward the good and provident **God**. To that place (if God wills) my own soul must go immediately. 

But regarding what **Simmias** had said earlier—that the soul is the **harmony** of the **body** <term>harmony (harmonia): the theory that the soul is not a distinct substance, but a musical-like balance of the body's physical tensions</term>, and that it would perish when the body died—**Socrates** refutes his opinion by a "reduction to absurdity" <note>original: *ab absurdo*. A logical move where you prove a statement is false by showing it leads to an impossible or ridiculous conclusion.</note>. 

If the soul were a harmony, Socrates says, it would follow that the soul did not exist before the body. However, it had already been granted and conceded [in the previous argument regarding recollection] that the soul exists before the body. Otherwise, since a harmony of this kind is formed from those things which are stretched and spread through the body (like the strings of an instrument), the harmony would have been formed before the very elements existed from which it was supposed to be composed.

Indeed, the arguments prove this sufficiently...

By the arguments we have used above, the **soul** <term>soul (anima): here referring to the animating principle that gives life to a physical body</term> is understood neither to be a product of, nor to depend upon the **temperament** <note>original: *temperamentum*. In medieval and Renaissance medicine, this refers to the "balance of humors" (blood, phlegm, etc.) that makes up the physical body.</note> of the body. Instead, it is separate from the body, unmixed, and **impassible** <note>original: *impassibilem*. A philosophical term meaning the soul cannot be affected or harmed by physical sensations or the decay of matter.</note>. Therefore, being ignorant of death, it descends into the body as the very principle of life in order to share life with it. Finally, having measured out the duration allotted to the nature of the body, it leaves the matter behind and remains immortal. Thus says **Socrates** in the *Cratylus*: *What do you think it is that holds and carries the nature of the entire body, so that it lives and moves about, other than the soul?* <note>original Greek: *Τὴν φύσιν παντὸς τοῦ σώματος ὥστε καὶ ζῆν καὶ περιϊέναι τί σοι δοκεῖ ἔχειν τε καὶ ὀχεῖν, ἄλλο ἢ ψυχή.*</note> That is to say: Is there anything that so contains and carries the nature of the whole body, so that it both lives and survives, other than the **soul**? <note>original Greek: *ἡ ψυχή* (hē psychē).</note> For this reason, it is called, as it were, *physeche* <note>The author is following Plato's wordplay in the *Cratylus*, suggesting that the word for soul (*psychē*) is derived from "holding nature" (*physis* + *echein*).</note>.

### So that it may embrace two figures.

**Plato**, in the *Timaeus*, compares the soul of man to a **triangle**, at the apex of which sits **Unity**. From one side descend the **even numbers**—2, 4, and 8—and from the other side the **odd numbers**—3, 9, and 27—descending down to the first cubic numbers. <note>This refers to the "Platonic Lambda," a diagram used to explain the mathematical proportions of the World Soul and the human soul, moving from a single point into three-dimensional reality.</note>

<note>A triangular diagram represents the Platonic Lambda, a sequence used in the *Timaeus* to explain the proportions of the World Soul. At the apex is the number 1. On the other hand, the number **twenty-seven**, as an odd and indivisible number, represents the **Incorruptible and eternal**, that is, the **ethereal vehicle** <note>The "starry" or celestial body of the soul, which remains immortal and carries the soul back to the heavens.</note>, in which the soul is clothed before it is finally cast into this **human prison-house** <note>original: *humanum ergastulum*. A classical metaphor for the physical body as a place of confinement or forced labor for the spirit.</note>. He says it is the same as if it were said that the soul consists of a certain **essence**...

# ON THE THIRTEENTH CHAPTER.

### *The soul of man is called by three names.*

In the book *The Soul of Wisdom* <note>original: *Anima sapientiæ*; likely referring to the Hebrew work *Nefesh Ha-Chakhmah*</note>, Rabbi Moses son of Shem-Tov <note>Moses de León, a 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist often associated with the Zohar.</note> says that there is only one soul in man, which is divided into three degrees:

<note>original Hebrew: הנפש נחלק לשלשה חלקים מתיחדים באחדותם: נפש: רוח: נשמה. והפילוסופים חלקו סוד הנפש בסוד שלש מדריגות וקראו אותם בשמותם כל אחת בסודה ועניינה: נפש הצומחת: נפש הבהמית: נפש השכלית.</note>

The soul is divided into three parts which are joined together in their unity: <term>Nephesh: the lower, vital soul associated with physical life and instincts.</term>; <term>Ruach: the middle soul or "spirit," associated with the emotions and the breath.</term>; <term>Neshamah: the highest, divine soul associated with the intellect and spiritual connection.</term>. Furthermore, the philosophers divided the mystery of the soul into a mystery of three degrees, and they called each by its name according to its secret and essence: the vegetative soul <note>governing growth and nutrition</note>; the animal soul <note>governing movement and sensation</note>; and the intellectual soul <note>governing reason</note>.

That is to say: The soul is divided into three parts, which are joined in their union: *Nephesh*, *Ruach*, *Neshamah*. The philosophers, however, divide the mystery of the soul into the mystery of three degrees, which they [call] by their names—

<vocab>Anima, Nephesch, Ruach, Neschamah, Rabbi Moses son of Shem-Tov, Soul of Wisdom</vocab>

<summary>This page begins the commentary on Chapter 13, defining the tripartite structure of the soul using both Kabbalistic terms (Nephesh, Ruach, Neshamah) and Aristotelian philosophical categories (vegetative, animal, intellectual).</summary>

...they designate each one according to its own mystery and property: **The vegetative soul; the animal soul; and the intellectual soul.** In Aristotle's second book *On the Soul*, chapter three <note>original: *de Anima cap. 3*</note>, the vegetative soul corresponds to a triangle; the sensing soul to a quadrangle; and the reasoning soul to a pentagon. And just as the quadrangle is potentially contained within the pentagon, and the triangle within the quadrangle, so in us the soul is one and simple in its essence, but multiple in its faculty and power. <note>Aristotle uses this geometric analogy to show how higher forms of life (like humans) contain the abilities of lower forms (like plants and animals) within them.</note>

### Nephesh.

*Nephesh* <note>The Hebrew term for the lowest level of the soul, often associated with the life force and physical existence.</note>, or the vegetative soul—or the desiring soul, as others prefer to call it—is mentioned in Deuteronomy 12:20: "Concerning the meat which the **soul** <note>original: **Nephesh**</note> desires." It has its seat in the liver, and it is nothing other than the soul clothed in a certain bodily spirit; by this medium, it is said to reside in the blood, according to Leviticus 17:14: "The **soul** <note>original: *Nephesh*</note> of all flesh is in the blood." And in Deuteronomy 12:23: "The blood is their soul."

<summary>This page explains the hierarchy of the soul using Aristotle's geometric analogies and identifies the 'Nephesh' (vegetative soul) as residing in the liver and blood.</summary>

...it is. That bodily spirit receives the life-giving spirit, as Rabbi Meir al-Dabi <note>A 14th-century Spanish Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> teaches in the book *The Paths of Faith* <note>original: *viæ fidei*, referring to the Hebrew work *Shevilei Emunah*</note>.

> The spirit of life is truly material; and it receives the vital spirit from the power of the Neshamah. <note>original: "רוח החיים הוא גשמי ממש: וקבל רוח חיונית מכח הנשמה."</note>

That is: The living spirit is bodily in a certain respect; however, it receives the life-giving spirit from the power of the <term>Neshamah (the highest, intellectual level of the soul)</term>. For this reason, that life-giving spirit is called in the scriptures the *Neshamat Chaim* <note>original: נשמת חיים</note>, the "breath of life." It is from this breath that the bodily spirit becomes a living thing, and from this it is named <term>Nephesh (the lowest or animal soul)</term>, as if it were *naphucha* <note>original: נפוחה</note>, meaning "diffused" or "blown out" by that life-giving spirit. This is according to Genesis 2:7: "And he breathed into his nostrils the **breath of life** <note>original: נשמת חיים / *neshamat chaim*</note>"; and then it immediately follows: "And man became a **living soul** <note>original: *Nephesh*</note>." This *Nephesh* is defined by Rabbi Moses ben Shem Tov <note>Commonly known as Moses de Leon, the 13th-century author associated with the Zohar.</note>:

> The power by which the body stands, and its senses. <note>original: "כח קיום הגוף והרגשותיו."</note>

That is: The power by which the body is sustained and its sensations exist. Rabbi Meir also attributes a sense to this *Nephesh* even after death—specifically, an internal sense.

> And although it has lost external sensation, it has not lost internal sensation. <note>original: "ואף על פי שהפסיד ההרגש החיצון לא הפסיד ההרגש הפנימי."</note>

That is: For even though the *Nephesh* is deprived...

This is: When people are pressed by necessity and distress, and they betake themselves to the graves; this <term>Nephesh</term> is awakened, and it wanders about and approaches the <term>Ruach</term> <note>The middle level of the soul, often translated as "spirit," associated with the emotions and breath.</note>: and with the <term>Ruach</term>, at certain times, the <term>Neshamah</term> <note>The highest, intellectual and most divine level of the soul.</note> is joined in the <term>bundle of the living</term> <note>original Latin: "fasciculo viventium"; a traditional Hebrew idiom (tzeror ha-chayyim) referring to the eternal resting place of the righteous with God.</note>: According to that passage in 1 Samuel chapter 25, verse 29: *The soul [Nephesh] of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living.* And it prays for the living; then it returns to its own place. There it celebrates the praises of God among the remains of the body: According to that passage in Psalm 35, verse 10: *All my bones shall say, "Lord, who is like unto you?"* Furthermore, in dreams, it warns people of the judgments that God decrees, according to that passage in Job 33, verse 15: *In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls upon men, while they slumber on their beds: then He opens the ears of men, and instructing them, He teaches them discipline.*

Regarding the souls <term>Nephesh</term> <note>original: *nephaschot* (plural); the lowest level of the soul associated with the physical body and animal life.</note> of the wicked, they say that some perish along with the body, according to that passage in **Leviticus 17:10**: *I will cut off that soul from among its people.* Others are said to linger around the corpses, and there, remembering their past lives, they groan: **Job 14:22**: *But his flesh shall have pain upon him, and his soul* <note>original Hebrew: ונפשו (*ve-naphsho*)</note>—*which is called the Nephesh—shall mourn over him.* They maintain that others are whirled about, according to that passage in **1 Samuel 25:29**: *The soul [Nephesh] of your enemies shall be slung out*, as if by the force and circle of a sling. It means that the spirit <note>The <term>Ruach</term>, or middle soul.</note> will not reside within it; for when the spirit has departed from it, that soul will have no communication with the higher realms, nor will it know anything of what happens in the world.

...of his previous life. The Platonists assert this very thing concerning the <term>Image of the soul</term> <note>original Latin: *Idolo animæ*; referring to the *eidolon*, a phantom or "shadow-self" that represents the personality and physical appearance of the deceased.</note>. Plotinus, in the *Enneads* <note>The collected writings of Plotinus, the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, book 4, part 3, chapter 27, says: "We must consider, I believe, that the phantom of **Hercules** in the underworld remembers everything that was done in life." Plato teaches this same principle universally concerning the soul in his dialogue, the *Gorgias*. **Death**, he says, is nothing other than the dissolution of two things: the **soul** and the **body**, so that they are separated from each other. Once this separation has been accomplished, each of them nevertheless separately preserves a certain state of its own—namely, the very same one with which the person was endowed while they lived. Therefore, the **body** preserves its nature, its physical features, and its characteristics; so that all these things remain visible in it. For example: if someone’s body had been large by nature, or through nourishment, or both, while he lived: even when he is dead, the **corpse** will be large. If it was stout while he was living, it will also be stout in death, and so on in the same way. Just as if someone were fond of styling their hair, they will also have hair when dead. And, to [sum up] the matter in a single word—

I might summarize: whatever the body of the person was like while living, all such things—or at least most of them—remain visible for a certain time in the corpse. I believe the very same thing, **Callicles** <note>A character in Plato’s dialogue *Gorgias* who argues that "might makes right."</note>, must be concluded regarding the soul. Surely everything in the soul will be conspicuous after it has been stripped of the body: all those things, I say, which are formed both by the power of nature and by the habits which a person, through the cultivation of specific matters, held in their soul while they lived.

### Ruach.

The Hebrews call the vehicle of the soul—whether one calls it the form or the shadow—the **Ruach** <note>original Hebrew: *Ruach* (רוּחַ), meaning spirit or breath; in Jewish mysticism, it is the middle level of the soul.</note>. They teach that it corresponds to the **Irascible power** <note>In medieval psychology, this is the "spirited" part of the soul responsible for courage, anger, and the will to overcome obstacles.</note>, and they define it as:

> The power that sustains the **Nephesh** <note>original Hebrew: *Nephesh* (נֶפֶשׁ); the lower, "animal" soul or vital life force that resides in the blood.</note> so that it may remain in the body. <note>original Hebrew: *Koach ha-mkayyem et ha-Nephesh l'hitkayyem ba-guf*.</note>

Indeed, when death follows: if a righteous Israelite passes away in the Land of Israel, his **Ruach** immediately enters the **double cave** <note>original Latin: *spelunca duplex*; a reference to the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron, where the Patriarchs are buried. In Kabbalistic tradition, this cave is a gateway between the physical world and the Garden of Eden.</note>, and...

Finally, they reach the Garden of Eden, where they are instructed by the forms of the higher Garden of Eden, devoting themselves to the contemplation of those things which they could not understand in this world due to the obstacles of the physical body; and at certain times, the soul ascends even higher.

That is: On the Sabbath days, and in every month and at fixed times, the **Ruach** <note>The "middle" soul or spirit, associated with the heart and moral virtues.</note> ascends upward, and there enjoys delights; afterward, it returns to its place. Thus it is written: *And the spirit returns to God who gave it.* <note>Ecclesiastes 12:7.</note> It surely returns at those times of which we speak.

### *Neshamah* <note>The highest of the three parts of the soul in Jewish mysticism, representing the divine spark or pure intellect.</note>

The *Neshamah* is defined by Rabbi Moses, son of Shem Tov <note>Referring to Moses de Leon (c. 1240–1305), the Spanish kabbalist associated with the Zohar.</note>, in the book *The Soul of Wisdom*: <note>original Hebrew: "Inyan ha-sekhel ha-amiti asher mi-mekor ha-chayyim nech-tzav mi-ma'ayan ha-sekhel ve-ha-chokhmah ba lishkon kavod ba-guf le-kayyem ha-kol la-avodat ha-bore yitbarakh."</note>

**That is:** The nature of the true intellect, hewn from the source of life and from the spring of intellect and wisdom, comes to establish its glory within the body, so that all things may be constantly directed toward the worship of the blessed God. At this point, we must remember that there is in reality only one soul in a human being, as we said above, which is distinguished according to different levels of power: <term>Neshamah</term> <note>the intellectual soul</note>, <term>Ruach</term> <note>the spirit or emotional soul</note>, and <term>Nephesh</term> <note>the vital or animal soul</note>. Thus, the soul understood according to its higher level (the level called the *Neshamah*) is said to go, after a person's death, to its own place, which is beneath the **Throne of Glory** <note>The "Throne of Glory" refers to the highest celestial realm in Jewish mysticism, the source of all souls.</note>; from there, it passes into the garden...

### Regarding Chapter Thirteen.

[The soul] is clothed in its own vehicle, in a shape similar to the shape of the body, through the process of **Formation** <note>original: "formationem" — referring to the world of *Yetzirah*.</note> from the level of **Beauty** <note>original: "gradu Decoris" — referring to the Sefirah *Tiferet* (Beauty), the central emotive sphere of the divine tree.</note>, from which it is named **Ruach** <term>Spirit</term>. Finally, in this world, through the process of **Making** <note>original: "factionem" — referring to the world of *Assiah*.</note> from the level of **Kingdom** <note>original: "gradu Regni" — referring to the Sefirah *Malkhut* (Kingdom), the lowest Sefirah that mediates between the divine and the physical.</note>, it is joined to the body by means of a certain corporeal spirit: from which it is called **Nephesh** <term>Vital Soul</term>. The Kabbalists express these four modes of the soul's levels of production with the abbreviation "ABYA" <note>אביע - An acronym for the four worlds of Kabbalistic cosmology: Atziluth (Emanation), Beriah (Creation), Yetzirah (Formation), and Assiah (Making/Action).</note>:

->**Atziluth: Beriah: Yetzirah: Assiah**<-
->**Emanation: Creation: Formation: Making**<-

They derive the concept of **Emanation** from Numbers 11:17: "And I will take <note>original: *ve-atzalti* (ואצלתי) — this Hebrew verb shares a root with *Atziluth* (Emanation).</note> of the spirit." However, they derive **Creation**, **Formation**, and **Making** from Isaiah 43:7:

->**Everyone who is called by my name, and for my glory: I created him; I formed him; I even made him.**<-
->כל הנקרא בשמי ולכבודי בראתיו; יצרתיו; אף עשיתיו.<-

That is: "Every person who calls upon my name, I have created him for my glory, I have formed him, and I have made him." Finally, at the time of the resurrection, making, formation, creation, and emanation will be united; and therefore so will the **Nephesh**, **Ruach**, and **Neshamah** <term>Intellectual Soul</term>. This is according to Isaiah 58:11: "And the Lord will give you rest always, and will fill your soul—which is called **Nephesh**—with splendors, and will set your bones free," as we read—

### They used to say it would have been better for man not to be created.

### But these [others] said it was better for man to have been created.

That is, for the soul to be united to the body. Plotinus, *Enneads* Book 2, Chapter 9, Section 17. "But if," he says, "they attach a body to the soul, it is clearly not so that the soul should suffer anything, but rather that it might grant to the other <note>Meaning the physical body or the material world.</note>—for it is wrong for envy to exist among the Gods—the ability to perceive individual things according to its capacity. Thus we shall understand that they provided for the world quite rightly, since..." <note>original Latin: "At ſi, inquit, animæ corpus annectant, non ita videlicet, vt hæc aliquid patiatur; ſed potius alteri largiatur (nefas eſt enim eſſe penes Deos inuidiam) ſingula pro facultate percipere..." This quote from Plotinus argues that the soul's descent into the body is an act of divine generosity and order, rather than a misfortune.</note>

### Philosophers call it the Material Intellect.

*Nephesh* <term>Nephesh|The Hebrew term for the "animal soul" or the lowest level of the soul, associated with biological life and physical desires.</term> is called the "material intellect" by the author of the *Binding* <note>Likely a reference to a specific philosophical commentary regarding the "ligation" or binding of the soul to the body.</note>, just as Averroës <term>Averroës|The Latin name for Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a famous Andalusian philosopher who sought to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Islam.</term> calls it the "Possible Intellect." It is termed "material" because it exists in a state of potentiality and relates to the Agent Intellect <term>Agent Intellect|The active, eternal mind that illuminates the human soul, turning potential knowledge into actual understanding.</term> in the same way that matter relates to form. Rabbi Meir al-Dabi in his book *Paths of Faith* <note>original Latin: *Viæ fidei*; this refers to the Hebrew work *Shevilei Emunah* by the 14th-century scholar Meir ben Isaac al-Dabi.</note> calls it "material" because it is drawn out from the potentiality of matter.

The soul is initially within the potentiality of the body's matter; and afterward the soul emerges from potentiality into actuality. <note>original Hebrew: הנפש היא מתחלה בכח חומר הגוף : ואחר כן תצא הנפש מן הכח אל הפועל.</note>

That is: The *Nephesh* is from the beginning in the potentiality of the body's matter: later the *Nephesh* exits from potentiality into action <term>actum|In Aristotelian philosophy, "actuality" (actus) is the state of being fully realized or functional, as opposed to "potentiality" (potentia).</term>.

However, more sensible philosophers call the "Possible Intellect" material not because it is drawn out of the potentiality of matter <meta>catchword: materiæ;</meta>

### *That the Soul is a Substance.*

## ON THE SIXTEENTH
## chapter.

### *That which is to be has already been named.* <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 6:10: "That which hath been is named already, and it is known that it is man."</note>

In the <term>Zohar</term> <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> section *Acharei Mot* <note>original Hebrew: אחרי מות, meaning 'After the death [of the sons of Aaron],' a portion of the Book of Leviticus.</note> column 109, regarding this passage from Ecclesiastes:

> All those souls of the children of men, before they descend to the world, are all engraved before Him in the firmament in that very same image that they have in this world; and all that they learn in this world, they knew entirely before they descended to the world. <note>This describes the concept of the "Pre-existence of Souls," suggesting that learning is a process of remembering divine knowledge lost at birth.</note>

That is: All the souls of men, before they descend into the world, are all described before God (blessed be He) in the firmament, in precisely that form which they will take in this world; and whatever they learn in this world, they already knew all these things before they came forth into the world.

# On the Sixteenth Chapter

For [God allows] others to remain in the shame of the world until they have been perfectly purged.

Some object: Since everyone undergoes judgment immediately after death, why is another judgment necessary? The Rabbis answer in the book *The Apple and the Flower* <note>original: *Pomum & flos*; likely referring to the Hebrew work *Tappuach ve-Nitzah*, a Kabbalistic commentary.</note>:

<note>original Hebrew: אף על פי שכבר נדונו לאחר מיתתם לגן עדן או לגיהנם מפני הנפש עדיין יהיה דין אחר אם יזכו לחיי עולם הבא שהוא קיים לעולם הבא.</note>
Even though they have already been judged after their death for the Garden of Eden or for <term>Gehenna</term> <note>The place of spiritual purification or punishment in Jewish tradition, often compared to purgatory or hell.</note> because of the soul, there will still be another judgment to determine if they will be worthy of the life of the world to come, which exists for the future world.

That is: Although they were judged after death, so that they might receive a bodily reward in the <term>Garden of Eden</term> <note>The spiritual paradise for the righteous after death.</note> through the <term>Nephesh</term> <note>The lowest part of the soul, associated with physical life and animal vitality.</note>; or suffer a bodily punishment in Gehenna; nevertheless, they will undergo another judgment: whether they are worthy of the eternal life of the world to come; so that they may enter the heavenly Jerusalem. This is what was said above: through this judgment the *Nephesh* is united <gloss>to the</gloss> <term>Ruach</term> <note>The middle level of the soul, associated with spirit, emotions, and moral breath.</note>, the *Ruach* <gloss>to the</gloss> <term>Neshamah</term> <note>The highest part of the soul, representing the divine intellect and the spark of God within humanity.</note>, and the *Neshamah* to God. Then finally God will renew the generations by giving a new spirit, etc. Recall what we wrote concerning the effect of the resurrection.

# Notes

David [said]: "I have prepared and lit a lamp for my Messiah" <note>original Latin: *Paravi, accendi lucernam Messiae meo*; a reference to Psalm 132:17</note>; that is, I have prepared the soul, for the soul is the lamp of God (Proverbs 20[:27]). Indeed, they say that the soul of David was the soul of the Messiah, which had previously been in Adam. From this, they tell the story that David lived no years other than the seventy remaining from the thousand years of Adam’s life <note>According to Midrashic tradition, Adam was destined to live 1,000 years but gifted 70 of them to King David, who otherwise would have had no life of his own.</note>. They designate this Kabbalistically through <term>Notaricon</term> <note>A Kabbalistic shorthand method where each letter of a word serves as an initial for another word or phrase.</note> in the name **Adam** (אדם): **A** designates Adam (א), **D** designates David (ד), and **M** designates the Messiah (מ).

However, it does not escape my notice that some have said the Messiah, the son of David, will come before the seventh millennium, as we read in the books *The Soul of Wisdom* <note>original: *Anima sapientiae*; likely referring to the Hebrew work *Nishmat Chochmah*.</note> and *The Merchant's Spices* <note>original: *Pulvis Aromatarius*; likely referring to the Hebrew work *Avqat Rokhel*.</note>. But the authors of both *The Soul of Wisdom* and *The Merchant's Spices* eventually conclude that it does not seem probable to them that the Messiah, the son of David, will come before the desolation of the seventh millennium. Because, they say, it would be necessary for all souls—if they had resumed their bodies by rising again at the arrival of the Messiah before the seventh millennium—to depart from them once more. ->The word *Et* [את]. *Through multiplication they become 9.*<-

# To carry out <gloss>statutes</gloss> Statutes, and to keep-
# keep <gloss>judgments</gloss> Judgments.

Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar whose work sought to harmonize Aristotelian philosophy with Torah study</note> in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Nevochim*</note>, part 3, chapter 26, says: "All commandments have a cause." This means that all commandments and prohibitions have a specific purpose and utility. For some, this use is known and manifest to us—such as the prohibition against murder and theft. For others, however, the purpose is not obvious to the common person, such as the commandments regarding garments made of mixed wool and linen <term>Sha'atnez; a biblical law prohibiting the weaving together of wool and linen in a single garment</term>; the prohibition of mixing meat and milk <note>A fundamental Jewish dietary law derived from the commandment not to "boil a kid in its mother's milk"</note>; the ritual of the goat sent into the wilderness <note>The Scapegoat of the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), which was symbolically laden with the sins of the people and cast off</note>; and likewise the laws concerning the foreskin <note>original: *praeputii*; likely referring here to *Orlah*, the prohibition against eating fruit from a tree during its first three years of growth</note> and heterogeneous mixtures <note>laws against interbreeding different species of animals or grafting different plants</note>. 

Those laws whose use and benefit are commonly known are called <gloss>judgments</gloss> Judgments <note>original: *Mishpatim*; laws that are logically necessary for a just society</note>. However, those whose use is not manifest to the general public are called <gloss>statutes</gloss> Statutes <note>original: *Chukkim*; divine decrees that bypass human reason</note>. Concerning these, our sages said: "Regarding the words which I <gloss>have decreed</gloss> decreed for you, you are not permitted to question them" (that is, to attempt to change them or to find fault with them). It is further said that Satan accuses them, and the Nations of the world contradict them <note>A traditional rabbinic teaching that because these laws (like the dietary laws or the red heifer) have no "rational" explanation, they are often mocked by those outside the faith or by one's own internal doubts (symbolized by Satan)</note>.

Maimonides, *Guide for the Perplexed*, Statutes, Judgments, Murder, theft, wool and linen, meat and milk, the Scapegoat, uncircumcised fruit, heterogeneous species.

<summary>This page explores Maimonides' distinction between 'Judgments' (rational social laws) and 'Statutes' (divine decrees with hidden purposes), arguing that even seemingly irrational laws have a divine cause.</summary>

## *From the affirmative commandments*
## *that are bound to time.*

<note>In Jewish law, these are known as "positive time-bound commandments." Generally, women are exempt from performing these specific ritual obligations that must be done at a particular time of day or year.</note>

For example, women are not bound <note>original: *obnoxiæ*</note> to dwell continually under the open sky during the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: *festa tabernaculorum*; the holiday of Sukkot, which involves living in temporary outdoor booths</note>.

# To carry out <gloss><note>Hebrew: chuqqim</note> statutes</gloss> and to keep <br/> <gloss><note>Hebrew: mishpatim</note> judgments</gloss>.

<margin>quickly... <note>original: *festo ver-*</note></margin>
Maimonides in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Neuochim*</note>, part 3, chapter 26, says: "All commandments have a cause." This means that all commandments and prohibitions have a purpose and a use, and in such a way that the use of some is known and manifest to us—such as the prohibition of murder <margin>M <note>Translator: likely an abbreviation for Maimonides</note></margin> and theft. For others, however, the use is not known, such as in the commandments regarding a garment mixed <margin>be... <note>fragment</note></margin> from wool and linen <note>the law of *shatnez*</note>; regarding meat and milk; regarding the goat <note>the Scapegoat of Leviticus 16</note> that was sent out into the wilderness; and likewise in the prohibition of the foreskin <note>referring to circumcision</note> and of diverse kinds <note>original: *heterogeneorum*; the law of *kilayim*, which prohibits mixing certain seeds or animal species</note>. Those whose use and utility are known <margin>where theft... <note>original: *vbi fur-*</note></margin> to the common people are called <gloss><note>Hebrew: mishpatim</note> judgments</gloss>; but those whose use is not manifest to the common people are called <gloss><note>Hebrew: chuqqim</note> statutes</gloss>. Regarding these, our Sages have said: "Concerning the words that <gloss>I have decreed <note>original: *chaqaqti*</note></gloss> for you, you are not permitted to reflect upon them" (that is, to change anything or to find fault with them); and "Satan accuses them, and the nations of the world gainsay them" <note>This refers to the idea that irrational-seeming laws are often the target of external criticism or internal doubt.</note>.

## ON CHAPTER NINETEEN.

->*Or that a single commandment may suffice.*<-

Understand the commandment: "You shall not covet," according to the author of the book *The Powder of the Merchant* <note>original: *Puluis Aromatarius*; this refers to the Hebrew work *Abkat Rokhel* by Machir ben Isaac Sarug, which discusses the afterlife and the significance of the commandments.</note>:

> At the beginning of His words, He made them hear the Ten Commandments <note>literally "ten words," a common Hebrew designation for the Decalogue</note> and sealed them with the commandment "You shall not covet," for all of them depend upon it. This hints that whoever fulfills this commandment, it is as if he fulfilled the entire Torah; and whoever transgresses it, it is as if he transgresses the entire Torah.

That is: He made them heirs of His words, and pronounced in their hearing the Ten Commandments <note>original: *decem verba*</note>, which He sealed with the commandment *You shall not covet*: for all things depend on it. This signifies that whoever observes this commandment, it is just as if he observed the whole law; and he who transgresses it, it is just as if he [transgressed] the whole law...

<summary>This page argues that the Tenth Commandment ("You shall not covet") is the most vital of the Decalogue, serving as a "seal" that contains the essence of all other laws. By citing the Hebrew work Abkat Rokhel, the author suggests that controlling internal desire is equivalent to upholding the entire legal and moral framework of the Torah.</summary>

### *Whether you consider the nourishment.*

Thus says <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher (c. 204–270 CE) and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works, the *Enneads*, were highly influential in blending philosophy with mystical thought.</note> in the *Enneads*, Book 3, Treatise 1, Chapter 1: <note>The original text provides this quote first in Greek and then in Latin.
