God forbid that a **Torah Scroll** <term>Torah Scroll: *Sefer Torah*. The most sacred object in Judaism, containing the five books of Moses.</term> in the Ark should depend on the stars! 

Rather, "everything depends on **Destiny**" refers to the **Supreme Crown** <term>Supreme Crown: *Keter Elyon*. In Kabbalah, the highest of the ten Sefirot (divine emanations), representing the Divine Will that exists above the laws of nature and the stars.</term>, from which all the constellations and flows descend. And even the Torah scroll in the Ark relates to **Beauty** <term>Beauty: *Tiferet*. The central Sefirah, often associated with the Written Torah and the harmony of the divine attributes.</term>. 

And so it is written in the **Zohar** <term>Zohar: The foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</term> in the portion of *Phinehas*: "Children, life, and sustenance do not depend on merit, but rather they depend on **Destiny**" <note>original: *mazla*. And behold, we see that Abraham saw in his own destiny <note>Referring to his astrological chart or natural fate.</note> that he was not destined to have a son. But the Holy One, blessed be He, brought him outside, as it is written: "And He brought him outside and said: 'Look now toward heaven...'" <note>Genesis 15:5.</note> Our Sages explained this as: "Go out from your **astrology** <term>Astrology: *Aztagninut*. The practice of reading the stars to determine fate.</term>!"

Come and see: all the creatures of the world, before the **Torah** was given to Israel, were dependent on the stars. This even included children, life, and sustenance. But after the **Torah** was given to Israel, it released them from the obligations of the stars and constellations. 

We learn this from Abraham, because his children were destined to receive the five books of the **Torah**. It was said concerning this: "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created" <note>Genesis 2:4. The Hebrew word for 'when they were created' (*be-hibaram*) contains the same letters as 'for Abraham' (*be-Abraham*), a classic mystical connection.</note>. Although "Night" is a proper name within the **celestial system**, that system has no dominion over **Israel**, who are called **"Man"** <term>Adam: Here used as a spiritual title for those who transcend animalistic or purely physical nature through the Torah.</term> in the manner mentioned previously <note>A reference to the principle "Ein Mazal le-Yisrael"—that the Jewish people are not bound by the stars when they connect to a higher spiritual reality.</note>.

The author of the **Akedat Yitzchak** <note>original: "Ba'al Akedah," referring to Rabbi Isaac Arama (c. 1420–1494), a prominent Spanish Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note> elaborated on this in the **Portion of Matot** and the **Portion of Ha'azinu**. The word "**afflicted**" <term>Ani: Usually translated as "poor," but the Hebrew root implies "affliction" or "lowliness."</term> is an expression of suffering. Even if a person possesses great **wealth**, if he is plagued by **sickness and disease**, he is called "afflicted." Or, if his **children** cause him distress and grief every day, he is "afflicted"—how much more so for one who is poor and must wander from place to place.

However, I say that this statement also comes to hint at something else. The vast majority of the tens of thousands who pursue **temporal desires**, wealth, and **imaginary honor**—for every single one of them exalts himself to say, "**I shall rule!**" <note>A reference to 1 Kings 1:5. # The Author’s Apology for Composing his Work According to
## The Zohar:

And it happened, when the Lord brought the **Book of the Zohar** <note>original: "Sefer ha-Zohar," the foundational work of Jewish mystical thought, or Kabbalah, traditionally attributed to the 2nd-century sage Shimon bar Yochai.</note> before me, that I saw within it many explanations and matters that were deep and more precious than pearls, yet they were scattered and dispersed. They are hidden and stored away, held in the depths of the abyss <note>A metaphor for the complexity and difficulty of accessing the Zohar's non-linear wisdom.</note> within the aforementioned book, following the order of the subject matter appropriate to it.

By this I mean that every single verse belonging to that specific **Torah portion**, <term>Parashah: one of the weekly sections into which the Five Books of Moses are divided for public reading.</term> as well as ancient words spoken from the mouths of the elders—<note>original: "vatikin," referring to the pious scholars of old who were meticulous in their worship and study.</note> that is to say, the explanations of the verses of the Holy Scriptures—are scattered and separated throughout the volumes of the book. There is no single "house" <note>A central location or organizational structure where all relevant commentaries are gathered.</note> where the entire order has been set down, and the place where these teachings reside and the place of their glory is unknown: one is here and another is there. 

And not only this, but no explanation was found at all for many of the weekly portions, such as *Matot*, *Masei*, *Ki Tavo*, *Nitzavim*, and *Berakhah*. <note>These are specific sections from the biblical books of Numbers and Deuteronomy. These are all the words of the **Holy Lamp**, <term>Holy Lamp: An Aramaic title (Butzina Kadisha) for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the 2nd-century sage to whom the Zohar is traditionally attributed.</term> for his words are both revealed and hidden, and not every man’s hand is equal in them. The investigative sages have already likened this matter to a wealthy man to whom a person came to lodge, both he and his animals. The wealthy man gave the traveler all kinds of delicacies to eat, and to his animals he gave straw and fodder; to each and every one he gave the thing appropriate for it. 

Is it not so that the holy **Rashbi**, <note>An acronym for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.</note> the **Lamp of Radiance**, <term>Lamp of Radiance: An Aramaic title (Butzina de-Nehora) emphasizing the sage's role in illuminating the mysteries of the Torah.</term> expanded in revealed allegories according to the weakness of the intellect of the masses, while also hinting at **secret** <note>original: "sod," the deepest level of interpretation in the Pardes system.</note> matters for the masters of the mystery, the Kabbalists? <meta>This page continues the author’s introduction, specifically detailing his methodology for compiling this work. The interpretation of the **Zohar** <term>Zohar: The "Splendor," the foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</term> which are found in his book (of blessed memory) <note>original: "z"l," an abbreviation for "zichrono livracha," of blessed memory.</note> are found scattered and separated <insert>▭</insert> one here and one there, as was mentioned. For my intention in this composition is to make it accessible to every person who has an open mind like my own, or even less than mine <insert>▭</insert> so that their reach is equal to others in understanding words of insight. 

My desire is the explanation of every matter according to the way of the **plain meaning** <term>Peshat: The literal or direct meaning of a text.</term> and the way of the **Midrash** <term>Midrash: A method of interpreting biblical stories through homilies, ethics, or legal deductions.</term> as mentioned. And for the deep **Kabbalists**, I did not feel the need to gather and compose deep matters of Kabbalah for them, because they are the minority, and the Torah said: **"Follow the majority."** <note>original: "acharei rabbim le-hatot" (Exodus 23:2). And even if you find many holy verses from the words of <insert>▭</insert> ranging from a mere hint up to the **Secret**, I did not refrain from gathering and joining them together for two reasons. The first reason is that for the holy man, **Rashbi** <term>Rashbi: An acronym for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the 2nd-century sage and traditional author of the Zohar.</term>, all of his words are both revealed and hidden. It is as he himself (of blessed memory) wrote in the Torah portion of **Beha’alotcha**: <term>Beha’alotcha: A section of the Book of Numbers (8:1–12:16) in the Torah.</term> 

And these are his words: **"Woe to the man who says that this Torah comes [only] to show worldly stories and the words of commoners,"** etc. <note>original: "Woe to the son of man who says that the Torah comes to show worldly stories..." Furthermore, this name is justified regarding both the **revealed** <term>Nigleh: The exoteric or literal aspects of Torah study accessible to all.</term> and the **hidden** <term>Nistar: The esoteric or mystical dimensions of Torah study, such as Kabbalah.</term>.

And although we intended in this work to gather and join together—as if with loops <note>original: "lula'ot." A biblical metaphor referring to the loops used to couple the curtains of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26:5), suggesting a seamless connection between different parts of a holy text.</note>—the verses of Holy Scripture <term>Mikra'ei Kodesh: A formal name for the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh).</term> that are interpreted through the plain, literal method <term>Peshat: The literal or direct meaning of a biblical text, as opposed to its allegorical or mystical interpretations.</term>; in truth, they are righteous together, and together they shall form a complete bond between the "Revealed" and the "Hidden" <term>Nigleh and Nistar: "Nigleh" (the revealed) refers to the literal and legalistic aspects of Torah, while "Nistar" (the hidden) refers to its mystical and esoteric dimensions, such as Kabbalah.</term>. The reason for this is well-known.

Furthermore, anyone who searches for and requests a certain thing is not considered "complete" or "whole" as long as that sought-after thing is not in his possession; for the very thing he desires is missing from him. Only when it is found with him is he then called "whole and complete." Therefore, once all the verses of the Holy Scriptures—which are otherwise scattered throughout all the books of the *Zohar* <term>Zohar: The "Book of Splendor," the foundational work of Jewish mysticism or Kabbalah.</term>—are collected and joined, each in its proper place, the seeker’s goal will be "whole." There he will find what he seeks, which until now has not been easily found with ease.

And so that it may be easy for anyone seeking an explanation for any verse from the Torah, the Prophets, or the Writings <note>original: "Torah, Nevi'im, and Ketuvim," the three sections of the Hebrew Bible, collectively known by the acronym Tanakh.</note>, I have placed markers at the end of the book. There I have recorded, in brief, the ultimate purpose of every verse and what it discusses. I have also included the teachings of our Sages of blessed memory <term>RaZaL: An acronym for "Rabbotenu Zichronam Livracha," the Jewish scholars and rabbis of antiquity.</term> explained therein, to demonstrate the utility of this volume. These are marked with the signs A, B, C, and so on. Similarly, for every verse, I have recorded a "place-guide" <term>Moreh Makom: A citation or reference index used to help readers find the source of a quote.</term> from the *Zohar* so that one may know its source—on which page and which side <note>In Hebrew printing, pages are often referred to as "leaves," with "side A" (folio recto) and "side B" (folio verso).</note> it is found—if perhaps the reader desires...
